senses.d: The hook on the end of an eccentric rod opposite the strap. See. Illust. of Eccentric.
The mouth; hence, idle prate; chatter; unmeaning talk; loquaciousness.

Gab.etym: [OE. gabbe gabble, mocking, fr. Icel. gabb mocking, mockery, or OF. gab, gabe; perh. akin to E. gape, or gob. Cf. Gab, v. i., Gibber.]

senses.d: To deceive; to lie.
To talk idly; to prate; to chatter.

Gab.etym: [OE. gabben to jest, lie, mock, deceive, fr. Icel. gabba to mock, or OF. gaber. See 2d Gab, and cf. Gabble.]

senses.d: The point of a spear, or an arrowhead.
A pointed or wedge-shaped instrument of metal, as a steel wedge used in mining, etc.
q: I will go get a leaf of brass, And with a gad of steel will write these words.

senses.d: A sharp-pointed rod; a goad.
A spike on a gauntlet; a gadling.
A wedge-shaped billet of iron or steel.
q: Flemish steel . . . some in bars and some in gads.

senses.d: A rod or stick, as a fishing rod, a measuring rod, or a rod used to drive cattle with.

Gad.etym: [OE. gad, Icel. gaddr goad, sting; akin to Sw. gadd sting, Goth. gazds, G. gerte switch. See Yard a measure.]

senses.d: To walk about; to rove or go about, without purpose; hence, to run wild; to be uncontrolled.
q: Why gaddest thou about so much to change thy way?

Gad.etym: [Prob. fr. gad, n., and orig. meaning to drive about.]

senses.d: A small British fish (Motella argenteola) of the Cod family.
A pike, so called at Moray Firth; — called also gead.
A square or beveled notch cut out of a girder, binding joist, or other timber which supports a floor beam, so as to receive the end of the floor beam.
Convenient; suitable; direct; near; handy; dexterous; easy; profitable; cheap; respectable.

Gain.etym: [OE. gein, gain, good, near, quick; cf. Icel. gegn ready, serviceable, and gegn, adv., against, opposite. Cf. Ahain.]

senses.d: That which is gained, obtained, or acquired, as increase, profit, advantage, or benefit; — opposed to loss.
q: But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
Godliness with contentment is great gain.
Every one shall share in the gains.

senses.d: The obtaining or amassing of profit or valuable possessions; acquisition; accumulation.

Gain.etym: [OE. gain, gein, ga”hen, gain, advantage, Icel. gagn; akin to Sw. gagn, Dan. gavn, cf. Goth. gageigan to gain. The word was prob. influenced by F. gain gain, OF. gaain. Cf. Gain, v. t.]

senses.d: To get, as profit or advantage; to obtain or acquire by effort or labor; as, to gain a good living.
q: What is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
To gain dominion, or to keep it gained.
For fame with toil we gain, but lose with ease.

senses.d: To come off winner or victor in; to be successful in; to obtain by competition; as, to gain a battle; to gain a case at law; to gain a prize.
To draw into any interest or party; to win to one's side; to conciliate.
q: If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
To gratify the queen, and gained the court.

senses.d: To reach; to attain to; to arrive at; as, to gain the top of a mountain; to gain a good harbor.
q: Forded Usk and gained the wood.

senses.d: To get, incur, or receive, as loss, harm, or damage.
q: Ye should . . . not have loosed from Crete, and to have gained this harm and loss.

Gain.syn: To obtain; acquire; get; procure; win; earn; attain; achieve.
Gain.etym: [From gain, n. but. prob. influenced by F. gagner to earn, gain, OF. gaaignier to cultivate, OHG. weidinōn, weidinen to pasture, hunt, fr. weida pasturage, G. weide, akin to Icel. veiðr hunting, AS. wāðu, cf. L. venari to hunt, E. venison. See Gain, n., profit.]

senses.d: To have or receive advantage or profit; to acquire gain; to grow rich; to advance in interest, health, or happiness; to make progress; as, the sick man gains daily.
q: Thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbors by extortion.
My good behavior had so far gained on the emperor, that I began to conceive hopes of liberty.

senses.d: To contradict; to deny; to controvert; to dispute; to forbid.
q: I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.
The just gods gainsay That any drop thou borrow'dst from thy mother, My sacred aunt, should by my mortal sword Be drained.

Gainsay.etym: [OE. geinseien, ageinseien. See Again, and Say to utter.]

senses.d: One who gainsays, contradicts, or denies.
Of or pertaining to Galatia or its inhabitants. — A native or inhabitant of Galatia, in Asia Minor; a descendant of the Gauls who settled in Asia Minor.
A strong current of air; a wind between a stiff breeze and a hurricane. The most violent gales are called tempests.
A moderate current of air; a breeze.
q: A little gale will soon disperse that cloud.
And winds of gentlest gale Arabian odors fanned From their soft wings.

senses.d: A state of excitement, passion, or hilarity.
q: The ladies, laughing heartily, were fast getting into what, in New England, is sometimes called a gale.

Gale.etym: [Prob. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. gal furious, Icel. galinn, cf. Icel. gala to sing, AS. galan to sing, Icel. galdr song, witchcraft, AS. galdor charm, sorcery, E. nightingale; also, Icel. gjōla gust of wind, gola breeze. Cf. Yell.]

senses.d: To sale, or sail fast.
A song or story.
To sing.
A plant of the genus Myrica, growing in wet places, and strongly resembling the bayberry. The sweet gale (Myrica Gale) is found both in Europe and in America.
The payment of a rent or annuity.
Of or pertaining to Galileo; as, the Galilean telescope. See Telescope.
Of or relating to Galilee.

Galilean.etym: [L. Galilaeus, fr. Galilaea Galilee, Gr. �: cf. F. galiléen.]

senses.d: A native or inhabitant of Galilee, the northern province of Palestine under the Romans.
One of the party among the Jews, who opposed the payment of tribute to the Romans; — called also Gaulonite.
A Christian in general; — used as a term of reproach by Mohammedans and Pagans.

A porch or waiting room, usually at the west end of an abbey church, where the monks collected on returning from processions, where bodies were laid previous to interment, and where women were allowed to see the monks to whom they were related, or to hear divine service. Also, frequently applied to the porch of a church, as at Ely and Durham cathedrals.

Galilee.etym: [Supposed to have been so termed in allusion to the scriptural “Galilee of the Gentiles.” cf. OF. galilée.]

senses.d: The bitter, alkaline, viscid fluid found in the gall bladder, beneath the liver. It consists of the secretion of the liver, or bile, mixed with that of the mucous membrane of the gall bladder.
The gall bladder.
Anything extremely bitter; bitterness; rancor.
q: He hath . . . compassed me with gall and travail.
Comedy diverted without gall.

senses.d: Impudence; brazen assurance.

Gall.etym: [OE. galle, gal, AS. gealla; akin to D. gal, OS. & OHG. galla, Icel. gall, SW. galla, Dan. galde, L. fel, Gr. �, and prob. to E. yellow. √49. See Yellow, and cf. Choler]

senses.d: An excrescence of any form produced on any part of a plant by insects or their larvae. They are most commonly caused by small Hymenoptera and Diptera which puncture the bark and lay their eggs in the wounds. The larvae live within the galls. Some galls are due to aphids, mites, etc. See Gallnut.

Gall.etym: [F. galle, noix de galle, fr. L. galla.]

senses.d: To impregnate with a decoction of gallnuts.
To fret and wear away by friction; to hurt or break the skin of by rubbing; to chafe; to injure the surface of by attrition; as, a saddle galls the back of a horse; to gall a mast or a cable.
q: I am loth to gall a new-healed wound.

senses.d: To fret; to vex; as, to be galled by sarcasm.
q: They that are most galled with my folly, They most must laugh.

senses.d: To injure; to harass; to annoy; as, the troops were galled by the shot of the enemy.
q: In our wars against the French of old, we used to gall them with our longbows, at a greater distance than they could shoot their arrows.

Gall.etym: [OE. gallen; cf. F. galer to scratch, rub, gale scurf, scab, G. galle a disease in horses' feet, an excrescence under the tongue of horses; of uncertain origin. Cf. Gall gallnut.]

senses.d: To scoff; to jeer.
A wound in the skin made by rubbing.
Showy; splendid; magnificent; gay; well-dressed.
q: The town is built in a very gallant place.
Our royal, good and gallant ship.

senses.d: Noble in bearing or spirit; brave; high-spirited; courageous; heroic; magnanimous; as, a gallant youth; a gallant officer.
q: That gallant spirit hath aspired the clouds.
The gay, the wise, the gallant, and the grave.

Gallant.etym: [F. gallant, prop. p. pr. of OF. galer to rejoice, akin to OF. gale amusement, It. gala ornament; of German origin; cf. OHG. geil merry, luxuriant, wanton, G. geil lascivious, akin to AS. g�l wanton, wicked, OS. g�l merry, Goth. gailjan to make to rejoice, or perh. akin to E. weal. See Gala, Galloon

senses.d: Polite and attentive to ladies; courteous to women; chivalrous.
A man of mettle or spirit; a gay, fashionable man; a young blood.
One fond of paying attention to ladies.
One who wooes; a lover; a suitor; in a bad sense, a seducer.
To attend or wait on, as a lady; as, to gallant ladies to the play.
To handle with grace or in a modish manner; as, to gallant a fan.
A long and narrow corridor, or place for walking; a connecting passageway, as between one room and another; also, a long hole or passage excavated by a boring or burrowing animal.
A room for the exhibition of works of art; as, a picture gallery; hence, also, a large or important collection of paintings, sculptures, etc.

A long and narrow platform attached to one or more sides of public hall or the interior of a church, and supported by brackets or columns; — sometimes intended to be occupied by musicians or spectators, sometimes designed merely to increase the capacity of the hall.
A frame, like a balcony, projecting from the stern or quarter of a ship, and hence called stern gallery or quarter gallery, — seldom found in vessels built since 1850.
Any communication which is covered overhead as well as at the sides. When prepared for defense, it is a defensive gallery.
A working drift or level.

Gallery.etym: [F. galerie, It. galleria, fr. LL. galeria gallery, perh. orig., a festal hall, banquetting hall; cf. OF. galerie a rejoicing, fr. galer to rejoice. Cf. Gallant, a.]

senses.d: A vessel propelled by oars, whether having masts and sails or not
The cookroom or kitchen and cooking apparatus of a vessel; — sometimes on merchant vessels called the caboose.
An oblong oven or muffle with a battery of retorts; a gallery furnace.
An oblong tray of wood or brass, with upright sides, for holding type which has been set, or is to be made up, etc.

Galley.etym: [OE. gale, galeie (cf. OF. galie, galée, LL. galea, LGr. �; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: To fright or terrify. See Gally, v. t.
A frame from which is suspended the rope with which criminals are executed by hanging, usually consisting of two upright posts and a crossbeam on the top; also, a like frame for suspending anything.
q: So they hanged Haman on the gallows.
If I hang, I'll make a fat pair of gallows.
O, there were desolation of gaolers and gallowses!

senses.d: A wretch who deserves the gallows.
The rest for the tympan when raised.
A pair of suspenders or braces.
q: At length him nailéd on a gallow tree.

Gallows.etym: [OE. galwes, pl., AS. galga, gealga, gallows, cross; akin to D. galg gallows, OS. & OHG. galgo, G. galgen, Icel. gālgi, Sw. & Dan. galge, Goth. galga a cross. Etymologically and historically considered, gallows is a noun in the plural number, but it is used as a singular, and hence is preceded by a;

senses.d: An opening in anything made by breaking or parting; as, a gap in a fence; an opening for a passage or entrance; an opening which implies a breach or defect; a vacant space or time; a hiatus; a mountain pass.
q: Miseries ensued by the opening of that gap.
It would make a great gap in your own honor.

Gap.etym: [OE. gap; cf. Icel. gap an empty space, Sw. gap mouth, breach, abyss, Dan. gab mouth, opening, AS. geap expanse; as adj., wide, spacious. See Gape.]

senses.d: To notch, as a sword or knife.
To make an opening in; to breach.
q: Their masses are gapp'd with our grape.

senses.d: The vertical distance between two superposed surfaces, esp. in a biplane.
To open the mouth wide
q: She stretches, gapes, unglues her eyes, And asks if it be time to rise.

senses.d: Showing self-forgetfulness in surprise, astonishment, expectation, etc.
q: With gaping wonderment had stared aghast.

senses.d: Manifesting a desire to injure, devour, or overcome.
q: They have gaped upon me with their mouth.

senses.d: To pen or part widely; to exhibit a gap, fissure, or hiatus.
q: May that ground gape and swallow me alive!

senses.d: To long, wait eagerly, or cry aloud for something; — with for, after, or at.
q: The hungry grave for her due tribute gapes.

Gape.syn: To gaze; stare; yawn. See Gaze.
Gape.etym: [OE. gapen, AS. geapan to open; akin to D. gapen to gape, G. gaffen, Icel. & Sw. gapa, Dan. gabe; cf. Skr. jabh to snap at, open the mouth. Cf. Gaby, Gap.]

senses.d: The act of gaping; a yawn.
The width of the mouth when opened, as of birds, fishes, etc.
A piece of ground appropriated to the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables.
A rich, well-cultivated spot or tract of country.
q: I am arrived from fruitful Lombardy, The pleasant garden of great Italy.

Garden.etym: [OE. gardin, OF. gardin, jardin, F. jardin, of German origin; cf. OHG. garto, G. garten; akin to AS. geard. See Yard an inclosure.]

senses.d: To lay out or cultivate a garden; to labor in a garden; to practice horticulture.
To cultivate as a garden.
One who makes and tends a garden; a horticulturist.
The crown of a king.
A wreath of chaplet made of branches, flowers, or feathers, and sometimes of precious stones, to be worn on the head like a crown; a coronal; a wreath.
The top; the thing most prized.
A book of extracts in prose or poetry; an anthology.
q: They began to be collected into little miscellanies under the name of garlands.

senses.d: A sort of netted bag used by sailors to keep provision in.

Garland.etym: [OE. garland, gerlond, OF. garlande, F. guirlande; of uncertain origin; cf. OHG. wiara, wiera, crown, pure gold, MHG. wieren to adorn.]

senses.d: To deck with a garland.
Any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, etc.
q: No man putteth a piece of new cloth unto old garment.

Garment.etym: [OE. garnement, OF. garnement, garniment, fr. garnir to garnish. See Garnish.]

senses.d: A granary; a building or place where grain is stored for preservation.

Garner.etym: [OE. garner, gerner, greiner, OF. gernier, grenier, F. grenier, fr. L. granarium, fr. granum. See 1st Grain, and cf. Granary.]

senses.d: To gather for preservation; to store, as in a granary; to treasure.
To decorate with ornamental appendages; to set off; to adorn; to embellish.
q: All within with flowers was garnished.

senses.d: To ornament, as a dish, with something laid about it; as, a dish garnished with parsley.
To furnish; to supply.
To fit with fetters.
To warn by garnishment; to give notice to; to garnishee. See Garnishee, v. t.

Garnish.etym: [OE. garnischen, garnissen, OF. garnir to provide, strengthen, prepare, garnish, warn, F. garnir to provide, furnish, garnish, — of German origin; cf. OHG. warnōn to provide, equip; akin to G. wahren to watch, E. aware, ware, wary, and cf. also E. warn. See Wary, -ish, and cf. Garment, Garrison.]

senses.d: Something added for embellishment; decoration; ornament; also, dress; garments, especially such as are showy or decorated.
q: So are you, sweet, Even in the lovely garnish of a boy.
Matter and figure they produce; For garnish this, and that for use.

senses.d: Something set round or upon a dish as an embellishment. See Garnish, v. t., 2.
Fetters.
A fee; specifically, in English jails, formerly an unauthorized fee demanded by the old prisoners of a newcomer.
A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town.
A fortified place, in which troops are quartered for its security.

Garrison.etym: [OE. garnisoun, F. garnison garrison, in OF. & OE. also, provision, munitions, from garnir to garnish. See Garnish.]

senses.d: To place troops in, as a fortification, for its defense; to furnish with soldiers; as, to garrison a fort or town.
To secure or defend by fortresses manned with troops; as, to garrison a conquered territory.
A large door or passageway in the wall of a city, of an inclosed field or place, or of a grand edifice, etc.; also, the movable structure of timber, metal, etc., by which the passage can be closed.
An opening for passage in any inclosing wall, fence, or barrier; or the suspended framework which closes or opens a passage. Also, figuratively, a means or way of entrance or of exit.
q: Knowest thou the way to Dover? Both stile and gate, horse way and footpath.
Opening a gate for a long war.

senses.d: A door, valve, or other device, for stopping the passage of water through a dam, lock, pipe, etc.
The places which command the entrances or access; hence, place of vantage; power; might.
q: The gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

senses.d: In a lock tumbler, the opening for the stump of the bolt to pass through or into.
The channel or opening through which metal is poured into the mold; the ingate.

Gate.etym: [OE. ”et, ”eat, giat, gate, door, AS. geat, gat, gate, door; akin to OS., D., & Icel. gat opening, hole, and perh. to E. gate a way, gait, and get, v. Cf. Gate a way, 3d Get.]

senses.d: To supply with a gate.
To punish by requiring to be within the gates at an earlier hour than usual.
A way; a path; a road; a street (as in Highgate).
q: I was going to be an honest man; but the devil has this very day flung first a lawyer, and then a woman, in my gate.

senses.d: Manner; gait.

Gate.etym: [Icel. gata; akin to SW. gata street, lane, Dan. gade, Goth. gatwö, G. gasse. Cf. Gate a door, Gait.]

senses.d: To bring together; to collect, as a number of separate things, into one place, or into one aggregate body; to assemble; to muster; to congregate.
q: And Belgium's capital had gathered them Her beauty and her chivalry.
When he had gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people together.

senses.d: To pick out and bring together from among what is of less value; to collect, as a harvest; to harvest; to cull; to pick off; to pluck.
q: A rose just gathered from the stalk.
Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?
Gather us from among the heathen.

senses.d: To accumulate by collecting and saving little by little; to amass; to gain; to heap up.
q: He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor.
To pay the creditor . . . he must gather up money by degrees.

senses.d: To bring closely together the parts or particles of; to contract; to compress; to bring together in folds or plaits, as a garment; also, to draw together, as a piece of cloth by a thread; to pucker; to plait; as, to gather a ruffle.
q: Gathering his flowing robe, he seemed to stand In act to speak, and graceful stretched his hand.

senses.d: To derive, or deduce, as an inference; to collect, as a conclusion, from circumstances that suggest, or arguments that prove; to infer; to conclude.
q: Let me say no more! Gather the sequel by that went before.

senses.d: To gain; to win.
q: He gathers ground upon her in the chase.

senses.d: To bring together, or nearer together, in masonry, as where the width of a fireplace is rapidly diminished to the width of the flue, or the like.
To haul in; to take up; as, to gather the slack of a rope.

Gather.etym: [OE. gaderen, AS. gaderian, gadrian, fr. gador, geador, together, fr. gæd fellowship; akin to E. good, D. gaderen to collect, G. gatte husband, MHG. gate, also companion, Goth. gadiliggs a sister's son. √29. See Good, and cf. Together.]

senses.d: To come together; to collect; to unite; to become assembled; to congregate.
q: When small humors gather to a gout.
Tears from the depth of some divine despair Rise in the heart, and gather to the eyes.

senses.d: To grow larger by accretion; to increase.
q: Their snowball did not gather as it went.

senses.d: To concentrate; to come to a head, as a sore, and generate pus; as, a boil has gathered.
To collect or bring things together.
q: Thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strewed.

senses.d: A plait or fold in cloth, made by drawing a thread through it; a pucker.
The inclination forward of the axle journals to keep the wheels from working outward.
The soffit or under surface of the masonry required in gathering. See Gather, v. t., 7.
One who gathers or collects.
An attachment for making gathers in the cloth.
The act of collecting or bringing together.
That which is gathered, collected, or brought together
Assembling; collecting; used for gathering or concentrating.
Excited with merriment; manifesting sportiveness or delight; inspiring delight; livery; merry.
q: Belinda smiled, and all the world was gay.
Gay hope is theirs by fancy fed.

senses.d: Brilliant in colors; splendid; fine; richly dressed.
q: Why is my neighbor's wife so gay?
A bevy of fair women, richly gay In gems and wanton dress!

senses.d: Loose; dissipated; lewd.

Gay.syn: Merry; gleeful; blithe; airy; lively; sprightly, sportive; light-hearted; frolicsome; jolly; jovial; joyous; joyful; glad; showy; splendid; vivacious.
Gay.etym: [F. gai, perhaps fr. OHG. g�hi swift, rapid, G. gäh, jäh, steep, hasty; or cf. OHG. w�hi beatiful, good. Cf. Jay.]

senses.d: An ornament
To fix the eyes in a steady and earnest look; to look with eagerness or curiosity, as in admiration, astonishment, or with studious attention.
q: Why stand ye gazing up into heaven?

Gaze.etym: [OE. gasen, akin to dial. Sw. gasa, cf. Goth. us-gaisjan to terrify, us-geisnan to be terrified. Cf. Aghast, Ghastly, Ghost, Hesitate.]

senses.d: To view with attention; to gaze on.
q: And gazed a while the ample sky.

senses.d: A fixed look; a look of eagerness, wonder, or admiration; a continued look of attention.
q: With secret gaze Or open admiration him behold.

senses.d: The object gazed on.
q: Made of my enemies the scorn and gaze.
I that rather held it better men should perish one by one, Than that earth should stand at gaze like Joshua's moon in Ajalon!

senses.d: One who gazes.
A person or thing gazed at with scorn or abhorrence; an object of curiosity or contempt.
The European pike.
Kind; sort.
Sex, male or female.
A classification of nouns, primarily according to sex; and secondarily according to some fancied or imputed quality associated with sex.
q: Gender is a grammatical distinction and applies to words only. Sex is natural distinction and applies to living objects.

Gender.etym: [OF. genre, gendre (with excrescent d.), F. genre, fr. L. genus, generis, birth, descent, race, kind, gender, fr. the root of genere, gignere, to beget, in pass., to be born, akin to E. kin. See Kin, and cf. Generate, Genre, Gentle, Genus.]

senses.d: To beget; to engender.

Gender.etym: [OF. gendrer, fr. L. generare. See Gender, n.]

senses.d: To copulate; to breed.
An account or history of the descent of a person or family from an ancestor; enumeration of ancestors and their children in the natural order of succession; a pedigree.
Regular descent of a person or family from a progenitor; pedigree; lineage.

Genealogy.etym: [OE. genealogi, genelogie, OF. genelogie, F. généalogie, L. genealogia, fr. Gr. �; � birth, race, descent (akin to L. genus) + � discourse.]

senses.d: Relating to a genus or kind; pertaining to a whole class or order; as, a general law of animal or vegetable economy.
Comprehending many species or individuals; not special or particular; including all particulars; as, a general inference or conclusion.
Not restrained or limited to a precise import; not specific; vague; indefinite; lax in signification; as, a loose and general expression.
Common to many, or the greatest number; widely spread; prevalent; extensive, though not universal; as, a general opinion; a general custom.
q: This general applause and cheerful shout Argue your wisdom and your love to Richard.

senses.d: Having a relation to all; common to the whole; as, Adam, our general sire.
As a whole; in gross; for the most part.
q: His general behavior vain, ridiculous.

senses.d: Usual; common, on most occasions; as, his general habit or method.

General.etym: [F. général, fr. L. generalis. See Genus.]

senses.d: The whole; the total; that which comprehends or relates to all, or the chief part; — opposed to particular.
q: In particulars our knowledge begins, and so spreads itself by degrees to generals.

senses.d: One of the chief military officers of a government or country; the commander of an army, of a body of men not less than a brigade. In European armies, the highest military rank next below field marshal.
The roll of the drum which calls the troops together; as, to beat the general.
The chief of an order of monks, or of all the houses or congregations under the same rule.
The public; the people; the vulgar.
In general; commonly; extensively, though not universally; most frequently.
In a general way, or in general relation; in the main; upon the whole; comprehensively.
q: Generally speaking, they live very quietly.

senses.d: Collectively; as a whole; without omissions.
q: I counsel that all Israel be generally gathered unto thee.

senses.d: The act of generating or begetting; procreation, as of animals.
Origination by some process, mathematical, chemical, or vital; production; formation; as, the generation of sounds, of gases, of curves, etc.
That which is generated or brought forth; progeny; offspiring.

A single step or stage in the succession of natural descent; a rank or remove in genealogy. Hence: The body of those who are of the same genealogical rank or remove from an ancestor; the mass of beings living at one period; also, the average lifetime of man, or the ordinary period of time at which one rank follows another, or father is succeeded by child, usually assumed to be one third of a century; an age.
q: This is the book of the generations of Adam.
Ye shall remain there many years, and for a long season, namely, seven generations.
All generations and ages of the Christian church.

senses.d: Race; kind; family; breed; stock.
q: Thy mother's of my generation; what's she, if I be a dog?

senses.d: The formation or production of any geometrical magnitude, as a line, a surface, a solid, by the motion, in accordance with a mathematical law, of a point or a magnitude; as, the generation of a line or curve by the motion of a point, of a surface by a line, a sphere by a semicircle, etc.
The aggregate of the functions and phenomene which attend reproduction.
Gentle; noble; of gentle birth.
q: All of a knight was fair and gent.

senses.d: Neat; pretty; fine; elegant.
q: Her body gent and small.

Gent.etym: [OF. gent, fr. L. genitus born, or (less prob.) fr. gentilis. See Genteel.]

senses.d: Gentle.
One of a non-Jewish nation; one neither a Jew nor a Christian; a worshiper of false gods; a heathen.

Gentile.etym: [L. gentilis belonging to the same clan, stock, race, people, or nation; in opposition to Roman, a foreigner; in opposition to Jew or Christian, a heathen: cf. F. gentil. See Gentle, a.]

senses.d: Belonging to the nations at large, as distinguished from the Jews; ethnic; of pagan or heathen people.
Denoting a race or country; as, a gentile noun or adjective.
Well-born; of a good family or respectable birth, though not noble.
q: British society is divided into nobility, gentry, and yeomanry, and families are either noble, gentle, or simple.
The studies wherein our noble and gentle youth ought to bestow their time.

senses.d: Quiet and refined in manners; not rough, harsh, or stern; mild; meek; bland; amiable; tender; as, a gentle nature, temper, or disposition; a gentle manner; a gentle address; a gentle voice.
A compellative of respect, consideration, or conciliation; as, gentle reader.
Not wild, turbulent, or refractory; quiet and docile; tame; peaceable; as, a gentle horse.
Soft; not violent or rough; not strong, loud, or disturbing; easy; soothing; pacific; as, a gentle touch; a gentle gallop .
q: O sleep! it is a gentle thing.

Gentle.syn: Mild; meek; placid; dovelike; quiet; peaceful; pacific; bland; soft; tame; tractable; docile.
Gentle.etym: [OE. gentil, F. gentil noble, pretty, graceful, fr. L. gentilis of the same clan or race, fr. gens, gentis, tribe, clan, race, orig. that which belongs together by birth, fr. the root of genere, gignere, to beget; hence gentle, properly, of birth or family, that is, of good or noble birth. See Gende

senses.d: One well born; a gentleman.
q: Gentles, methinks you frown.

senses.d: A trained falcon. See Falcon-gentil.
A dipterous larva used as fish bait.
To make genteel; to raise from the vulgar; to ennoble.
To make smooth, cozy, or agreeable.
q: To gentle life's descent, We shut our eyes, and think it is a plain.

senses.d: To make kind and docile, as a horse.
The quality or state of being gentle, well-born, mild, benevolent, docile, etc.; gentility; softness of manners, disposition, etc.; mildness.
In a gentle manner.
q: My mistress gently chides the fault I made.

senses.d: A small coin and weight; 1-20th of a shekel.
Jet, the mineral.
Fashion; manner; custom.
Artifice; contrivance.

To procure; to obtain; to gain possession of; to acquire; to earn; to obtain as a price or reward; to come by; to win, by almost any means; as, to get favor by kindness; to get wealth by industry and economy; to get land by purchase, etc.
Hence, with have and had, to come into or be in possession of; to have.
q: Thou hast got the face of man.

senses.d: To beget; to procreate; to generate.
q: I had rather to adopt a child than get it.

senses.d: To obtain mental possession of; to learn; to commit to memory; to memorize; as to get a lesson; also with out; as, to get out one's Greek lesson.
q: It being harder with him to get one sermon by heart, than to pen twenty.

senses.d: To prevail on; to induce; to persuade.
q: Get him to say his prayers.

senses.d: To procure to be, or to cause to be in any state or condition; — with a following participle.
q: Those things I bid you do; get them dispatched.

senses.d: To betake; to remove; — in a reflexive use.
q: Get thee out from this land.
He . . . got himself . . . to the strong town of Mega.

Get.syn: To obtain; gain; win; acquire. See Obtain.
Get.etym: [OE. geten, AS. gitan, gietan (in comp.); akin to Icel. geta, Goth. bigitan to find, L. prehendere to seize, take, Gr. χανδάνειν to hold, contain. Cf. Comprehend, Enterprise, Forget, Impregnable, Prehensile.]

senses.d: To make acquisition; to gain; to profit; to receive accessions; to be increased.
q: We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they daily get.

senses.d: To arrive at, or bring one's self into, a state, condition, or position; to come to be; to become; — with a following adjective or past participle belonging to the subject of the verb; as, to get sober; to get awake; to get beaten; to get elected.
q: To get rid of fools and scoundrels.
His chariot wheels get hot by driving fast.

senses.d: Offspring; progeny; as, the get of a stallion.
the original third pers. sing. pres. of Go.
The act of obtaining or acquiring; acquisition.
q: With all thy getting, get understanding.

senses.d: That which is got or obtained; gain; profit.
The spirit; the soul of man.
q: Then gives her grieved ghost thus to lament.

senses.d: The disembodied soul; the soul or spirit of a deceased person; a spirit appearing after death; an apparition; a specter.
q: The mighty ghosts of our great Harrys rose.
I thought that I had died in sleep, And was a blessed ghost.

senses.d: Any faint shadowy semblance; an unsubstantial image; a phantom; a glimmering; as, not a ghost of a chance; the ghost of an idea.
q: Each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.

senses.d: A false image formed in a telescope by reflection from the surfaces of one or more lenses.
q: And he gave up the ghost full softly.
Jacob . . . yielded up the ghost, and was gathered unto his people

Ghost.etym: [OE. gast, gost, soul, spirit, AS. gāst breath, spirit, soul; akin to OS. g�st spirit, soul, D. geest, G. geist, and prob. to E. gaze, ghastly.]

senses.d: To die; to expire.
To appear to or haunt in the form of an apparition.
A man of extraordinari bulk and stature.
q: Giants of mighty bone and bold emprise.

senses.d: A person of extraordinary strength or powers, bodily or intellectual.
Any animal, plant, or thing, of extraordinary size or power.

Giant.etym: [OE. giant, geant, geaunt, OF. jaiant, geant, F. géant, L. gigas, fr. Gr. �, �, from the root of E. gender, genesis. See Gender, and cf. Gigantic.]

senses.d: Like a giant; extraordinary in size, strength, or power; as, giant brothers; a giant son.
To guide. See Gye .
To give.
Anything given; anything voluntarily transferred by one person to another without compensation; a present; an offering.
q: Shall I receive by gift, what of my own, . . . I can command ?

senses.d: The act, right, or power of giving or bestowing; as, the office is in the gift of the President.
A bribe; anything given to corrupt.
q: Neither take a gift, for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise.

senses.d: Some quality or endowment given to man by God; a preëminent and special talent or aptitude; power; faculty; as, the gift of wit; a gift for speaking.
A voluntary transfer of real or personal property, without any consideration. It can be perfected only by deed, or in case of personal property, by an actual delivery of possession.

Gift.syn: Present; donation; grant; largess; benefaction; boon; bounty; gratuity; endowment; talent; faculty.
Gift.etym: [OE. gift, yift, yeft, AS. gift, fr. gifan to give; akin to D. & G. gift, Icel. gift, gipt, Goth. gifts (in comp.). See Give, v. t.]

senses.d: To endow with some power or faculty.
q: He was gifted . . . with philosophical sagacity.

senses.d: Against; near by; towards; as, gin night.
If.
To begin; — often followed by an infinitive without to; as, gan tell. See Gan.

Gin.etym: [OE. ginnen, AS. ginnan (in comp.), prob. orig., to open, cut open, cf. OHG. inginnan to begin, open, cut open, and prob. akin to AS. gīnan to yawn, and E. yawn. √31. See Yawn, v. i., and cf. Begin.]

senses.d: A strong alcoholic liquor, distilled from rye and barley, and flavored with juniper berries; — also called Hollands and Holland gin, because originally, and still very extensively, manufactured in Holland. Common gin is usually flavored with turpentine.
Contrivance; artifice; a trap; a snare.
A machine for raising or moving heavy weights, consisting of a tripod formed of poles united at the top, with a windlass, pulleys, ropes, etc.
A machine for separating the seeds from cotton; a cotton gin.
To catch in a trap.
To clear of seeds by a machine; as, to gin cotton.
A stroke with a rod or switch; a severe spasm; a twinge; a pang.
q: Conscience . . . is freed from many fearful girds and twinges which the atheist feels.

senses.d: A cut; a sarcastic remark; a gibe; a sneer.
q: I thank thee for that gird, good Tranio.

senses.d: To strike; to smite.
q: To slay him and to girden off his head.

senses.d: To sneer at; to mock; to gibe.
q: Being moved, he will not spare to gird the gods.

Gird.etym: [See Gird, n., and cf. Girde, v.]

senses.d: To gibe; to sneer; to break a scornful jest; to utter severe sarcasms.
q: Men of all sorts take a pride to gird at me.

senses.d: To encircle or bind with any flexible band.
To make fast, as clothing, by binding with a cord, girdle, bandage, etc.
To surround; to encircle, or encompass.
q: That Nyseian isle, Girt with the River Triton.

senses.d: To clothe; to swathe; to invest.
q: I girded thee about with fine linen.
The Son . . . appeared Girt with omnipotence.

senses.d: To prepare; to make ready; to equip; as, to gird one's self for a contest.
q: Thou hast girded me with strength.

Gird.etym: [OE. girden, gurden, AS. gyrdan; akin to OS. gurdian, D. gorden, OHG. gurten, G. gürten, Icel. gyrða, Sw. gjorda, Dan. giorde, Goth. bigaírdan to begird, and prob. to E. yard an inclosure. Cf. Girth, n. & v., Girt, v. t.]

senses.d: That with which one is girded; a girdle.
q: Instead of a stomacher, a girding of sackcloth.

senses.d: A griddle.
That which girds, encircles, or incloses; a circumference; a belt; esp., a belt, sash, or article of dress encircling the body usually at the waist; a cestus.
q: Within the girdle of these walls.
Their breasts girded with golden girdles.

senses.d: The zodiac; also, the equator.
q: From the world's girdle to the frozen pole.
That gems the starry girdle of the year.

senses.d: The line ofgreatest circumference of a brilliant-cut diamond, at which it is grasped by the setting. See Illust. of Brilliant.
A thin bed or stratum of stone.
The clitellus of an earthworm.

Girdle.etym: [OE. gurdel, girdel, AS. gyrdel, fr. gyrdan; akin to D. gordel, G. gürtel, Icel. gyr�ill. See Gird, v. t., to encircle, and cf. Girth, n.]

senses.d: To bind with a belt or sash; to gird.
To inclose; to environ; to shut in.
q: Those sleeping stones, That as a waist doth girdle you about.

senses.d: To make a cut or gnaw a groove around (a tree, etc.) through the bark and alburnum, thus killing it.
A young person of either sex; a child.
A female child, from birth to the age of puberty; a young maiden.
A female servant; a maidservant.
A roebuck two years old.

Girl.etym: [OE. girle, gerle, gurle, a girl (in sense 1): cf. LG. gör child.]

senses.d: To gird; to encircle; to invest by means of a girdle; to measure the girth of; as, to girt a tree.
q: We here create thee the first duke of Suffolk, And girt thee with the sword.

senses.d: Bound by a cable; — used of a vessel so moored by two anchors that she swings against one of the cables by force of the current or tide.
Same as Girth.
To bestow without receiving a return; to confer without compensation; to impart, as a possession; to grant, as authority or permission; to yield up or allow.
q: For generous lords had rather give than pay.

senses.d: To yield possesion of; to deliver over, as property, in exchange for something; to pay; as, we give the value of what we buy.
q: What shall a man give in exchange for his soul ?

senses.d: To yield; to furnish; to produce; to emit; as, flint and steel give sparks.
To communicate or announce, as advice, tidings, etc.; to pronounce; to render or utter, as an opinion, a judgment, a sentence, a shout, etc.
To grant power or license to; to permit; to allow; to license; to commission.
q: It is given me once again to behold my friend.
Then give thy friend to shed the sacred wine.

senses.d: To exhibit as a product or result; to produce; to show; as, the number of men, divided by the number of ships, gives four hundred to each ship.

To devote; to apply; used reflexively, to devote or apply one's self; as, the soldiers give themselves to plunder; also in this sense used very frequently in the past participle; as, the people are given to luxury and pleasure; the youth is given to study.
To set forth as a known quantity or a known relation, or as a premise from which to reason; — used principally in the passive form given.
To allow or admit by way of supposition.
q: I give not heaven for lost.

senses.d: To attribute; to assign; to adjudge.
q: I don't wonder at people's giving him to me as a lover.

senses.d: To excite or cause to exist, as a sensation; as, to give offense; to give pleasure or pain.
To pledge; as, to give one's word.

Give.etym: [OE. given, yiven, yeven, AS. gifan, giefan; akin to D. geven, OS. geðan, OHG. geban, G. geben, Icel. gefa, Sw. gifva, Dan. give, Goth. giban. Cf. Gift, n.]

senses.d: To give a gift or gifts.
To yield to force or pressure; to relax; to become less rigid; as, the earth gives under the feet.
To become soft or moist.
To move; to recede.
q: Now back he gives, then rushes on amain.

senses.d: To shed tears; to weep.
q: Whose eyes do never give But through lust and laughter.

senses.d: To have a misgiving.
q: My mind gives ye're reserved To rob poor market women.

senses.d: To open; to lead.
q: This, yielding, gave into a grassy walk.

senses.d: To afford a view of; as, his window gave the park.
Granted; assumed; supposed to be known; set forth as a known quantity, relation, or premise.
Disposed; inclined; — used with an adv.; as, virtuously given.
Stated; fixed; as, in a given time.
One who gives; a donor; a bestower; a grantor; one who imparts or distributes.
q: It is the giver, and not the gift, that engrosses the heart of the Christian.

senses.d: The act of bestowing as a gift; a conferring or imparting.
A gift; a benefaction.
The act of softening, breaking, or yielding.
q: His givings out were of an infinite distance From his true meant design.

senses.d: Pleased; joyous; happy; cheerful; gratified; — opposed to sorry, sorrowful, or unhappy; — said of persons, and often followed by of, at, that, or by the infinitive, and sometimes by with, introducing the cause or reason.
q: A wise son maketh a glad father.
He that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished.
The Trojan, glad with sight of hostile blood.
He, glad of her attention gained.
As we are now glad to behold your eyes.
Glad am I that your highness is so armed.

senses.d: Wearing a gay or bright appearance; expressing or exciting joy; producing gladness; exhilarating.
q: Her conversation More glad to me than to a miser money is.
Glad evening and glad morn crowned the fourth day.

Glad.syn: Pleased; gratified; exhilarated; animated; delighted; happy; cheerful; joyous; joyful; cheering; exhilarating; pleasing; animating.
Glad.etym: [AS. glæd bright, glad; akin to D. glad smooth, G. glatt, OHG. glat smooth, shining, Icel. gla�r glad, bright, Dan. & Sw. glad glad, Lith. glodas smooth, and prob. to L. glaber, and E. glide. Cf. Glabrous.]

senses.d: To make glad; to cheer; to gladden; to exhilarate.
q: That which gladded all the warrior train.
Each drinks the juice that glads the heart of man.

Glad.etym: [AS. gladian. See Glad, a., and cf. Gladden, v. t.]

senses.d: To be glad; to rejoice.
Preferably; by choice.
With pleasure; joyfully; cheerfully; eagerly.
q: The common people heard him gladly.

senses.d: State or quality of being glad; pleasure; joyful satisfaction; cheerfulness.
q: They . . . did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart.
The Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day.

senses.d: A hard, brittle, translucent, and commonly transparent substance, white or colored, having a conchoidal fracture, and made by fusing together sand or silica with lime, potash, soda, or lead oxide. It is used for window panes and mirrors, for articles of table and culinary use, for lenses, and various articles of ornament.
Any substance having a peculiar glassy appearance, and a conchoidal fracture, and usually produced by fusion.
Anything made of glass.
q: She would not live The running of one glass.

senses.d: A drinking vessel; a tumbler; a goblet; hence, the contents of such a vessel; especially; spirituous liquors; as, he took a glass at dinner.
An optical glass; a lens; a spyglass; — in the plural, spectacles; as, a pair of glasses; he wears glasses.
A weatherglass; a barometer.

Glass.etym: [OE. glas, gles, AS. glæs; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. glas, Icel. glas, gler, Dan. glar; cf. AS. glær amber, L. glaesum. Cf. Glare, n., Glaze, v. t.]

senses.d: To reflect, as in a mirror; to mirror; — used reflexively.
q: Happy to glass themselves in such a mirror.
Where the Almighty's form glasses itself in tempests.

senses.d: To case in glass.
To cover or furnish with glass; to glaze.
To smooth or polish anything, as leater, by rubbing it with a glass burnisher.
To gather after a reaper; to collect in scattered or fragmentary parcels, as the grain left by a reaper, or grapes left after the gathering.
q: To glean the broken ears after the man That the main harvest reaps.

senses.d: To gather from (a field or vineyard) what is left.
To collect with patient and minute labor; to pick out; to obtain.
q: Content to glean what we can from . . . experiments.

Glean.etym: [OE. glenen, OF. glener, glaner, F. glaner, fr. LL. glenare; cf. W. glan clean, glanh�u to clean, purify, or AS. gelm, gilm, a hand�ul.]

senses.d: To gather stalks or ears of grain left by reapers.
q: And she went, and came, and gleaned in the field after the reapers.

senses.d: To pick up or gather anything by degrees.
q: Piecemeal they this acre first, then that; Glean on, and gather up the whole estate.

senses.d: A collection made by gleaning.
q: The gleans of yellow thyme distend his thighs.

senses.d: Cleaning; afterbirth.
The act of gathering after reapers; that which is collected by gleaning.
q: Glenings of natural knowledge.

senses.d: The common European kite (Milvus ictinus). This name is also sometimes applied to the buzzard.

Glede.etym: [AS. glida, akin to Icel. gleða, Sw. glada. Cf. Glide, v. i.]

senses.d: A live coal.
q: The cruel ire, red as any glede.

senses.d: To be bright; to sparkle; to be brilliant; to shine; to glisten; to glitter.
q: All that glisters is not gold.

Glister.etym: [OE. glistren; akin to G. glistern,glinstern, D. glinsteren, and E. glisten. See Glisten.]

senses.d: Glitter; luster.
To sparkle with light; to shine with a brilliant and broken light or showy luster; to gleam; as, a glittering sword.
q: The field yet glitters with the pomp of war.

senses.d: To be showy, specious, or striking, and hence attractive; as, the glittering scenes of a court.

Glitter.syn: To gleam; to glisten; to shine; to sparkle; to glare. See Gleam, Flash.
Glitter.etym: [OE. gliteren; akin to Sw. glittra, Icel. glitra, glita, AS. glitenian, OS. glītan, OHG. glīzzan, G. gleissen, Goth. glitmunjan, and also to E. glint, glisten, and prob. glance, gleam.]

senses.d: A bright, sparkling light; brilliant and showy luster; brilliancy; as, the glitter of arms; the glitter of royal equipage.
State of being gloomy.
Imperfectly illuminated; dismal through obscurity or darkness; dusky; dim; clouded; as, the cavern was gloomy.
Affected with, or expressing, gloom; melancholy; dejected; as, a gloomy temper or countenance.

Gloomy.syn: Dark; dim; dusky; dismal; cloudy; moody; sullen; morose; melancholy; sad; downcast; depressed; dejected; disheartened.

senses.d: To make glorious by bestowing glory upon; to confer honor and distinction upon; to elevate to power or happiness, or to celestial glory.
q: Jesus was not yet glorified.

senses.d: To make glorious in thought or with the heart, by ascribing glory to; to acknowledge the excellence of; to render homage to; to magnify in worship; to adore.
q: That we for thee may glorify the Lord.

Glorify.etym: [F. glorifier, L. glorificare; gloria glory + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See -fy.]

senses.d: Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory; noble; praiseworthy; excellent; splendid; illustrious; inspiring admiration; as, glorious deeds.
q: These are thy glorious works, Parent of good !

senses.d: Eager for glory or distinction; haughty; boastful; ostentatious; vainglorious.
q: Most miserable Is the desire that's glorious.

senses.d: Ecstatic; hilarious; elated with drink.
q: kings may be blest, but Tam was glorious, O'er all the ills of life victorious.
During his office treason was no crime, The sons of Belial had a glorious time.
Sing ye to the Lord, for he hath triumphed gloriously.
I speak it not gloriously, nor out of affectation.

Glorious.syn: Eniment; noble; excellent; renowned; illustrious; celebrated; magnificent; grand; splendid.
Glorious.etym: [OF. glorios, glorious, F. glorieux, fr. L. gloriosus. See Glory, n.]

senses.d: Praise, honor, admiration, or distinction, accorded by common consent to a person or thing; high reputation; honorable fame; renown.
q: Glory to God in the highest.
Spread his glory through all countries wide.

senses.d: That quality in a person or thing which secures general praise or honor; that which brings or gives renown; an object of pride or boast; the occasion of praise; excellency; brilliancy; splendor.
q: Think it no glory to swell in tyranny.
Jewels lose their glory if neglected.
Your sex's glory 't is to shine unknown.

senses.d: Pride; boastfulness; arrogance.
q: In glory of thy fortunes.

senses.d: The presence of the Divine Being; the manifestations of the divine nature and favor to the blessed in heaven; celestial honor; heaven.
q: Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory.

senses.d: An emanation of light supposed to proceed from beings of peculiar sanctity. It is represented in art by rays of gold, or the like, proceeding from the head or body, or by a disk, or a mere line.

Glory.etym: [OE. glorie, OF. glorie, gloire, F. gloire, fr. L. gloria; prob. akin to Gr. κλέοσ, Skr. çravas glory, praise, çru to hear. See Loud.]

senses.d: To exult with joy; to rejoice.
q: Glory ye in his holy name.

senses.d: To boast; to be proud.
q: God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.
No one . . . should glory in his prosperity.

Glory.etym: [OE. glorien, OF. glorier, fr. L. gloriari, fr. gloria glory. See Glory, n.]

senses.d: One who eats voraciously, or to excess; a gormandizer.
Fig.: One who gluts himself.
q: Gluttons in murder, wanton to destroy.

senses.d: A carnivorous mammal (Gulo luscus), of the family Mustelidæ, about the size of a large badger. It was formerly believed to be inordinately voracious, whence the name; the wolverene. It is a native of the northern parts of America, Europe, and Asia.

Glutton.etym: [OE. glotoun, glotun, F. glouton, fr. L. gluto, glutto. See Glut.]

senses.d: Gluttonous; greedy; gormandizing.
q: A glutton monastery in former ages makes a hungry ministry in our days.

senses.d: To glut; to eat voraciously.
q: Gluttoned at last, return at home to pine.
Whereon in Egypt gluttoning they fed.

senses.d: Given to gluttony; eating to excess; indulging the appetite; voracious; as, a gluttonous age.
To strike together, as in anger or pain; as, to gnash the teeth.

Gnash.etym: [OE. gnasten, gnaisten, cf. Icel. gnastan a gnashing, gn�sta to gnash, Dan. knaske, Sw. gnissla, D. knarsen, G. knirschen.]

senses.d: To grind or strike the teeth together.
q: There they him laid, Gnashing for anguish, and despite, and shame.

senses.d: A blood-sucking dipterous fly, of the genus Culex, undergoing a metamorphosis in water. The females have a proboscis armed with needlelike organs for penetrating the skin of animals. These are wanting in the males. In America they are generally called mosquitoes. See Mosquito.
Any fly resembling a Culex in form or habits; esp., in America, a small biting fly of the genus Simulium and allies, as the buffalo gnat, the black fly, etc.

To bite, as something hard or tough, which is not readily separated or crushed; to bite off little by little, with effort; to wear or eat away by scraping or continuous biting with the teeth; to nibble at.
q: His bones clean picked; his very bones they gnaw.

senses.d: To bite in agony or rage.
q: They gnawed their tongues for pain.

senses.d: To corrode; to fret away; to waste.

Gnaw.etym: [OE. gnawen, AS. gnagan; akin to D. knagen, OHG. gnagan, nagan, G. nagen, Icel. & Sw. gnaga, Dan. gnave, nage. Cf. Nag to tease.]

senses.d: To use the teeth in biting; to bite with repeated effort, as in eating or removing with the teeth something hard, unwieldy, or unmanageable.
q: I might well, like the spaniel, gnaw upon the chain that ties me.

senses.d: Gone.

To pass from one place to another; to be in motion; to be in a state not motionless or at rest; to proceed; to advance; to make progress; — used, in various applications, of the movement of both animate and inanimate beings, by whatever means, and also of the movements of the mind; also figuratively applied.
To move upon the feet, or step by step; to walk; also, to walk step by step, or leisurely.
To be passed on fron one to another; to pass; to circulate; hence, with for, to have currency; to be taken, accepted, or regarded.
q: The man went among men for an old man in the days of Saul.
should go according to its true value.

senses.d: To proceed or happen in a given manner; to fare; to move on or be carried on; to have course; to come to an issue or result; to succeed; to turn out.
q: How goes the night, boy ?
I think, as the world goes, he was a good sort of man enough.
Whether the cause goes for me or against me, you must pay me the reward.

senses.d: To proceed or tend toward a result, consequence, or product; to tend; to conduce; to be an ingredient; to avail; to apply; to contribute; — often with the infinitive; as, this goes to show.
q: Against right reason all your counsels go.
To master the foul flend there goeth some complement knowledge of theology.

senses.d: To apply one's self; to set one's self; to undertake.
q: Seeing himself confronted by so many, like a resolute orator, he went not to denial, but to justify his cruel falsehood.

senses.d: To proceed by a mental operation; to pass in mind or by an act of the memory or imagination; — generally with over or through.
q: By going over all these particulars, you may receive some tolerable satisfaction about this great subject.

senses.d: To be with young; to be pregnant; to gestate.
q: The fruit she goes with, I pray for heartily, that it may find Good time, and live.

senses.d: To move from the person speaking, or from the point whence the action is contemplated; to pass away; to leave; to depart; — in opposition to stay and come.
q: I will let you go, that ye may sacrifice to the Lord your God; . . . only ye shall not go very far away.

senses.d: To pass away; to depart forever; to be lost or ruined; to perish; to decline; to decease; to die.
q: By Saint George, he's gone! That spear wound hath our master sped.

senses.d: To reach; to extend; to lead; as, a line goes across the street; his land goes to the river; this road goes to New York.
q: His amorous expressions go no further than virtue may allow.

senses.d: To have recourse; to resort; as, to go to law.

Go.etym: [OE. gan, gon, AS. gān, akin to D. gaan, G. gehn, gehen, OHG. gēn, gān, SW. gå, Dan. gaae; cf. Gr. κιχάναι to reach, overtake, Skr. hā to go, AS. gangan, and E. gang. The past tense in AS., eode, is from the root i to go, as is also Goth. iddja went. √47a. Cf. Gang, v. i., Wend.]

senses.d: To take, as a share in an enterprise; to undertake or become responsible for; to bear a part in.
q: They to go equal shares in the booty.

senses.d: To bet or wager; as, I'll go you a shilling.
Act; working; operation.
q: So gracious were the goes of marriage.

senses.d: A circumstance or occurrence; an incident.
q: This is a pretty go.

senses.d: The fashion or mode; as, quite the go.
Noisy merriment; as, a high go.
A glass of spirits.
Power of going or doing; energy; vitality; perseverance; push; as, there is no go in him.
That condition in the course of the game when a player can not lay down a card which will not carry the aggregate count above thirty-one.
Something that goes or is successful; a success; as, he made a go of it; also, an agreement.
q: “Well,” said Fleming, “is it a go?”

senses.d: A species of antelope (Procapra picticauda), inhabiting Thibet.
A pointed instrument used to urge on a beast; hence, any necessity that urges or stimulates.
q: The daily goad urging him to the daily toil.

Goad.etym: [AS. gād; perh. akin to AS. gār a dart, and E. gore. See Gore, v. t.]

senses.d: To prick; to drive with a goad; hence, to urge forward, or to rouse by anything pungent, severe, irritating, or inflaming; to stimulate.
q: That temptation that doth goad us on.

Goad.syn: To urge; stimulate; excite; arouse; irritate; incite; instigate.

senses.d: A hollow-horned ruminant of the genus Capra, of several species and varieties, esp. the domestic goat (C. hircus), which is raised for its milk, flesh, and skin.

Goat.etym: [OE goot, got, gat, AS. gāt; akin to D. geit, OHG. geiz, G. geiss, Icel. geit, Sw. get, Dan. ged, Goth. gaits, L. haedus a young goat, kid.]

senses.d: The skin of a goat, or leather made from it.
Made of the skin of a goat.
Same as Goaf.
A little mass or collection; a small quantity; a mouthful.
The mouth.

Gob.etym: [OF. gob morsel; cf. F. gobe, gobbe, a poisoned morsel, poison ball, gobet a piece swallowed, gober to swallow greedily and without tasting; cf. Gael. & Ir. gob mouth, snout, W. gwp a bird's head and neck. Cf. Gobble, Job, n.]

senses.d: A kind of cup or drinking vessel having a foot or standard, but without a handle.
q: We love not loaded boards and goblets crowned.

Goblet.etym: [F. gobelet, LL. gobeletus, gobellus; cf. L. cupa tub, cask. See Cupel.]

senses.d: Good.
A being conceived of as possessing supernatural power, and to be propitiated by sacrifice, worship, etc.; a divinity; a deity; an object of worship; an idol.
q: He maketh a god, and worshipeth it.
The race of Israel . . . bowing lowly down To bestial gods.

senses.d: The Supreme Being; the eternal and infinite Spirit, the Creator, and the Sovereign of the universe; Jehovah.
q: God is a Spirit; and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.

senses.d: A person or thing deified and honored as the chief good; an object of supreme regard.
q: Whose god is their belly.

senses.d: Figuratively applied to one who wields great or despotic power.

God.etym: [AS. god; akin to OS. & D. god, OHG. got, G. gott, Icel. guð, goð, Sw. & Dan. gud, Goth. gup, prob. orig. a p. p. from a root appearing in Skr. hū, p. p. hūta, to call upon, invoke, implore. √30. Cf. Goodbye, Gospel, Gossip.]

senses.d: To treat as a god; to idolize.
A female god; a divinity, or deity, of the female sex.
q: When the daughter of Jupiter presented herself among a crowd of goddesses, she was distinguished by her graceful stature and superior beauty.

senses.d: A woman of superior charms or excellence.
Godship; deity; divinity; divine nature or essence; godhood.
The Deity; God; the Supreme Being.
q: The imperial throne Of Godhead, fixed for ever.

senses.d: A god or goddess; a divinity.
q: Adoring first the genius of the place, The nymphs and native godheads yet unknown.

senses.d: Careful observance of, or conformity to, the laws of God; the state or quality of being godly; piety.
q: Godliness is profitable unto all things.

senses.d: Pious; reverencing God, and his character and laws; obedient to the commands of God from love for, and reverence of, his character; conformed to God's law; devout; righteous; as, a godly life.
q: For godly sorrow worketh repentance.

senses.d: Piously; devoutly; righteously.
q: All that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.

senses.d: Haste; ardent desire to go.

Gog.etym: [Cf. agog, F. gogue sprightliness, also W. gogi to agitate, shake.]

senses.d: The act of moving in any manner; traveling; as, the going is bad.
Departure.
Pregnancy; gestation; childbearing.
Course of life; behavior; doings; ways.
q: His eyes are upon the ways of man, and he seeth all his goings.

senses.d: That goes; in existence; available for present use or enjoyment; current; obtainable; also, moving; working; in operation; departing; as, he is of the brightest men going; going prices or rate.
Carrying on its ordinary business; conducting business, or carried on, with an indefinite prospect of continuance; — chiefly used in the phrases a going business, concern, etc.
Of or pert. to a going business or concern; as, the going value of a company.
An old English name of some yellow flower, — the marigold (Calendula), according to Dr. Prior, but in Chaucer perhaps the turnsole.

A metallic element, constituting the most precious metal used as a common commercial medium of exchange. It has a characteristic yellow color, is one of the heaviest substances known (specific gravity 19.32), is soft, and very malleable and ductile. It is quite unalterable by heat, moisture, and most corrosive agents, and therefore well suited for its use in coin and jewelry. Symbol Au (Aurum). Atomic weight 196.7.
Money; riches; wealth.
q: For me, the gold of France did not seduce.

senses.d: A yellow color, like that of the metal; as, a flower tipped with gold.
Figuratively, something precious or pure; as, hearts of gold.

Gold.etym: [AS. gold; akin to D. goud, OS. & G. gold, Icel. gull, Sw. & Dan. guld, Goth. gulþ, Russ. & OSlav. zlato; prob. akin to E. yellow. √49, 234. See Yellow, and cf. Gild, v. t.]

senses.d: Made of gold; consisting of gold.
Having the color of gold; as, the golden grain.
Very precious; highly valuable; excellent; eminently auspicious; as, golden opinions.

Golden.etym: [OE. golden; cf. OE. gulden, AS. gylden, from gold. See Gold, and cf. Guilder.]

senses.d: An artisan who manufactures vessels and ornaments, etc., of gold.
A banker.
Calvary. See the Note under Calvary.
A man.

Gome.etym: [AS. guma; akin to Goth. guma, L. homo. See Bridegroom.]

senses.d: The black grease on the axle of a cart or wagon wheel; — called also gorm. See Gorm.
A Hebrew measure. See Homer.
A conical chamber at the breech of the bore in heavy ordnance, especially in mortars; — named after the inventor.

Possessing desirable qualities; adapted to answer the end designed; promoting success, welfare, or happiness; serviceable; useful; fit; excellent; admirable; commendable; not bad, corrupt, evil, noxious, offensive, or troublesome, etc.
q: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.
Good company, good wine, good welcome.

senses.d: Possessing moral excellence or virtue; virtuous; pious; religious; — said of persons or actions.
q: In all things showing thyself a pattern of good works.

senses.d: Kind; benevolent; humane; merciful; gracious; polite; propitious; friendly; well-disposed; — often followed by to or toward, also formerly by unto.
q: The men were very good unto us.

senses.d: Serviceable; suited; adapted; suitable; of use; to be relied upon; — followed especially by for.
q: All quality that is good for anything is founded originally in merit.

senses.d: Clever; skillful; dexterous; ready; handy; — followed especially by at.
q: He . . . is a good workman; a very good tailor.
Those are generally good at flattering who are good for nothing else.

senses.d: Adequate; sufficient; competent; sound; not fallacious; valid; in a commercial sense, to be depended on for the discharge of obligations incurred; having pecuniary ability; of unimpaired credit.
q: My reasons are both good and weighty.
My meaning in saying he is a good man is . . . that he is sufficient . . . I think I may take his bond.

senses.d: Real; actual; serious; as in the phrases in good earnest; in good sooth.
q: Love no man in good earnest.

senses.d: Not small, insignificant, or of no account; considerable; esp., in the phrases a good deal, a good way, a good degree, a good share or part, etc.
Not lacking or deficient; full; complete.
q: Good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over.

senses.d: Not blemished or impeached; fair; honorable; unsullied; as in the phrases a good name, a good report, good repute, etc.
q: A good name is better than precious ointment

Good.etym: [AS. Gōd, akin to D. goed, OS. gōd, OHG. guot, G. gut, Icel. gōðr, Sw. & Dan. god, Goth. gōds; prob. orig., fitting, belonging together, and akin to E. gather. √29 Cf. Gather.]

senses.d: That which possesses desirable qualities, promotes success, welfare, or happiness, is serviceable, fit, excellent, kind, benevolent, etc.; — opposed to evil.
q: There be many that say, Who will show us any good ?

senses.d: Advancement of interest or happiness; welfare; prosperity; advantage; benefit; — opposed to harm, etc.
q: The good of the whole community can be promoted only by advancing the good of each of the members composing it.

senses.d: Wares; commodities; chattels; — formerly used in the singular in a collective sense. In law, a comprehensive name for almost all personal property as distinguished from land or real property.
q: He hath made us spend much good.
Thy lands and goods Are, by the laws of Venice, confiscate Unto the state of Venice.

senses.d: Well, — especially in the phrase as good, with a following as expressed or implied; equally well with as much advantage or as little harm as possible.
q: As good almost kill a man as kill a good book.
They who counsel ye to such a suppressing, do as good as bid ye suppress yourselves.

senses.d: To make good; to turn to good.
To manure; to improve.
Beauty of form; grace; elegance; comeliness.
q: Her goodliness was full of harmony to his eyes.

senses.d: Excellently.
Pleasant; agreeable; desirable.
q: We have many goodly days to see.

senses.d: Of pleasing appearance or character; comely; graceful; as, a goodly person; goodly raiment, houses.
q: The goodliest man of men since born.

senses.d: Large; considerable; portly; as, a goodly number.
q: Goodly and great he sails behind his link.

Goodly.etym: [OE. godlich, AS. gōdlic. See Good, and Like.]

senses.d: A familiar appellation of civility, equivalent to “My friend”, “Good sir”, “Mister;” — sometimes used ironically.
q: With you, goodman boy, an you please.

senses.d: A husband; the master of a house or family; — often used in speaking familiarly.
q: Say ye to the goodman of the house, . . . Where is the guest-chamber ?

senses.d: The quality of being good in any of its various senses; excellence; virtue; kindness; benevolence; as, the goodness of timber, of a soil, of food; goodness of character, of disposition, of conduct, etc.
One of several North American burrowing rodents of the genera Geomys and Thomomys, of the family Geomyidæ; — called also pocket gopher and pouched rat. See Pocket gopher, and Tucan.

One of several western American species of the genus Spermophilus, of the family Sciuridæ; as, the gray gopher (Spermophilus Franklini) and the striped gopher (S. tridecemlineatus); — called also striped prairie squirrel, leopard marmot, and leopard spermophile. See Spermophile.
A large land tortoise (Testudo Carilina) of the Southern United States, which makes extensive burrows.
A large burrowing snake (Spilotes Couperi) of the Southern United States.
Dirt; mud.
Blood; especially, blood that after effusion has become thick or clotted.

Gore.etym: [AS. gor dirt, dung; akin to Icel. gor, SW. gorr, OHG. gor, and perh. to E. cord, chord, and yarn; cf. Icel. görn, garnir, guts.]

senses.d: A wedgeshaped or triangular piece of cloth, canvas, etc., sewed into a garment, sail, etc., to give greater width at a particular part.
A small traingular piece of land.
One of the abatements. It is made of two curved lines, meeting in an acute angle in the fesse point.

Gore.etym: [OE. gore, gare, AS. g�ra angular point of land, fr. g�r spear; akin to D. geer gore, G. gehre gore, ger spear, Icel. geiri gore, geir spear, and prob. to E. goad. Cf. Gar, n., Garlic, and Gore, v.]

senses.d: To pierce or wound, as with a horn; to penetrate with a pointed instrument, as a spear; to stab.
q: The low stumps shall gore His daintly feet.

Gore.etym: [OE. gar spear, AS. g�r. See 2d Gore.]

senses.d: To cut in a traingular form; to piece with a gore; to provide with a gore; as, to gore an apron.
Imposing through splendid or various colors; showy; fine; magnificent.
q: Cloud-land, gorgeous land.
Gorgeous as the sun at midsummer.

Gorgeous.etym: [OF. gorgias beautiful, glorious, vain, luxurious; cf. OF. gorgias ruff, neck handkerchief, and F. gorge throat, and se pengorger to assume airs. Cf. Gorge, n.]

senses.d: Glad tidings; especially, the good news concerning Christ, the Kingdom of God, and salvation.
q: And Jesus went about all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, and preaching the gospel of the kingdom.
The steadfast belief of the promises of the gospel.
Thus the literal sense [of gospel] is the “narrative of God,” i.e., the life of Christ.

senses.d: One of the four narratives of the life and death of Jesus Christ, written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
A selection from one of the gospels, for use in a religious service; as, the gospel for the day.
Any system of religious doctrine; sometimes, any system of political doctrine or social philosophy; as, this political gospel.
Anything propounded or accepted as infallibly true; as, they took his words for gospel.
q: If any one thinks this expression hyperbolical, I shall only ask him to read Œdipus, instead of taking the traditional witticisms about Lee for gospel.

Gospel.etym: [OE. gospel, godspel, AS. godspell; god God + spell story, tale. See God, and Spell, v.]

senses.d: Accordant with, or relating to, the gospel; evangelical; as, gospel righteousness.
To instruct in the gospel.

A fleshy, three-celled, many-seeded fruit, as the melon, pumpkin, cucumber, etc., of the order Cucurbitaceæ; and especially the bottle gourd (Lagenaria vulgaris) which occurs in a great variety of forms, and, when the interior part is removed, serves for bottles, dippers, cups, and other dishes.
A dipper or other vessel made from the shell of a gourd; hence, a drinking vessel; a bottle.

Gourd.etym: [F. gourde, OF. cougourde, gouhourde, fr. L. cucurbita gourd (cf. NPr. cougourdo); perh. akin to corbin basket, E. corb. Cf. Cucurbite.]

senses.d: A false die. See Gord.
A silver dollar; — so called in Cuba, Hayti, etc.
To direct and control, as the actions or conduct of men, either by established laws or by arbitrary will; to regulate by authority.
To regulate; to influence; to direct; to restrain; to manage; as, to govern the life; to govern a horse.
q: Govern well thy appetite.

senses.d: To require to be in a particular case; as, a transitive verb governs a noun in the objective case; or to require (a particular case); as, a transitive verb governs the objective case.

Govern.etym: [OF. governer, F. gouverner, fr. L. gubernare to steer, pilot, govern, Gr. κυβερνα̑ν. Cf. Gubernatorial.]

senses.d: To exercise authority; to administer the laws; to have the control.
The act of governing; the exercise of authority; the administration of laws; control; direction; regulation; as, civil, church, or family government.
The mode of governing; the system of polity in a state; the established form of law.
q: That free government which we have so dearly purchased, free commonwealth.

senses.d: The right or power of governing; authority.
q: I here resign my government to thee.

senses.d: The person or persons authorized to administer the laws; the ruling power; the administration.
q: When we, in England, speak of the government, we generally understand the ministers of the crown for the time being.

senses.d: The body politic governed by one authority; a state; as, the governments of Europe.
Management of the limbs or body.
The influence of a word in regard to construction, requiring that another word should be in a particular case.
One who governs; especially, one who is invested with the supreme executive authority in a State; a chief ruler or magistrate; as, the governor of Pennsylvania.
One who has the care or guardianship of a young man; a tutor; a guardian.
A pilot; a steersman.
A contrivance applied to steam engines, water wheels, and other machinery, to maintain nearly uniform speed when the resistances and motive force are variable.

Governor.etym: [OE. governor, governour, OF. governeor, F. gouverneur, fr. L. gubernator steersman, ruler, governor. See Govern.]

senses.d: The exercise of love, kindness, mercy, favor; disposition to benefit or serve another; favor bestowed or privilege conferred.
q: To bow and sue for grace With suppliant knee.

senses.d: The divine favor toward man; the mercy of God, as distinguished from His justice; also, any benefits His mercy imparts; divine love or pardon; a state of acceptance with God; enjoyment of the divine favor.
q: And if by grace, then is it no more of works.
My grace is sufficicnt for thee.
Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.
By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand.

senses.d: The prerogative of mercy execised by the executive, as pardon.
Fortune; luck; — used commonly with hard or sorry when it means misfortune.
Inherent excellence; any endowment or characteristic fitted to win favor or confer pleasure or benefit.
q: He is complete in feature and in mind. With all good grace to grace a gentleman.
I have formerly given the general character of Mr. Addison's style and manner as natural and unaffected, easy and polite, and full of those graces which a flowery imagination diffuses over writing.

senses.d: Beauty, physical, intellectual, or moral; loveliness; commonly, easy elegance of manners; perfection of form.
q: Grace in women gains the affections sooner, and secures them longer, than any thing else.
I shall answer and thank you again For the gift and the grace of the gift.

senses.d: Graceful and beautiful females, sister goddesses, represented by ancient writers as the attendants sometimes of Apollo but oftener of Venus. They were commonly mentioned as three in number; namely, Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia, and were regarded as the inspirers of the qualities which give attractiveness to wisdom, love, and social intercourse.
q: The Graces love to weave the rose.
The Loves delighted, and the Graces played.

senses.d: The title of a duke, a duchess, or an archbishop, and formerly of the king of England.
q: How fares your Grace !

senses.d: Thanks.
q: Yielding graces and thankings to their lord Melibeus.

senses.d: A petition for grace; a blessing asked, or thanks rendered, before or after a meal.
Ornamental notes or short passages, either introduced by the performer, or indicated by the composer, in which case the notation signs are called grace notes, appeggiaturas, turns, etc.
An act, vote, or decree of the government of the institution; a degree or privilege conferred by such vote or decree.

Grace.syn: Elegance; comeliness; charm; favor; kindness; mercy.
Grace.etym: [F. grâce, L. gratia, from gratus beloved, dear, agreeable; perh. akin to Gr. � to rejoice, � favor, grace, Skr. hary to desire, and E. yearn. Cf. Grateful, Gratis.]

senses.d: To adorn; to decorate; to embellish and dignify.
q: Great Jove and Phoebus graced his noble line.
We are graced with wreaths of victory.

senses.d: To dignify or raise by an act of favor; to honor.
q: He might, at his pleasure, grace or disgrace whom he would in court.

senses.d: To supply with heavenly grace.
To add grace notes, cadenzas, etc., to.
Abounding in grace or mercy; manifesting love, or bestowing mercy; characterized by grace; beneficent; merciful; disposed to show kindness or favor; condescending; as, his most gracious majesty.
q: A god ready to pardon, gracious and merciful.
So hallowed and so gracious in the time.

senses.d: Abounding in beauty, loveliness, or amiability; graceful; excellent.
q: Since the birth of Cain, the first male child, . . . There was not such a gracious creature born.

senses.d: Produced by divine grace; influenced or controlled by the divine influence; as, gracious affections.

Gracious.syn: Favorable; kind; benevolent; friendly; beneficent; benignant; merciful.

senses.d: In a gracious manner; courteously; benignantly.
Fortunately; luckily.
A German title of nobility, equivalent to earl in English, or count in French. See Earl.
A steward; an overseer.
q: is nothing but a servant, overseer, or graff, and not the head, which is a title belonging only to Christ.

senses.d: A single small hard seed; a kernel, especially of those plants, like wheat, whose seeds are used for food.
The fruit of certain grasses which furnish the chief food of man, as corn, wheat, rye, oats, etc., or the plants themselves; — used collectively.
q: Storehouses crammed with grain.

senses.d: Any small, hard particle, as of sand, sugar, salt, etc.; hence, any minute portion or particle; as, a grain of gunpowder, of pollen, of starch, of sense, of wit, etc.
q: I . . . with a grain of manhood well resolved.

senses.d: The unit of the English system of weights; — so called because considered equal to the average of grains taken from the middle of the ears of wheat. 7,000 grains constitute the pound avoirdupois, and 5,760 grains the pound troy. A grain is equal to .0648 gram. See Gram.
A reddish dye made from the coccus insect, or kermes; hence, a red color of any tint or hue, as crimson, scarlet, etc.; sometimes used by the poets as equivalent to Tyrian purple.
q: All in a robe of darkest grain.
Doing as the dyers do, who, having first dipped their silks in colors of less value, then give' them the last tincture of crimson in grain.

senses.d: The composite particles of any substance; that arrangement of the particles of any body which determines its comparative roughness or hardness; texture; as, marble, sugar, sandstone, etc., of fine grain.
q: Hard box, and linden of a softer grain.

senses.d: The direction, arrangement, or appearance of the fibers in wood, or of the strata in stone, slate, etc.
q: Knots, by the conflux of meeting sap, Infect the sound pine and divert his grain Tortive and errant from his course of growth.

senses.d: The fiber which forms the substance of wood or of any fibrous material.
The hair side of a piece of leather, or the marking on that side.
The remains of grain, etc., after brewing or distillation; hence, any residuum. Also called draff.
A rounded prominence on the back of a sepal, as in the common dock. See Grained, a., 4.
Temper; natural disposition; inclination.
q: Brothers . . . not united in grain.

Grain.etym: [F. grain, L. granum, grain, seed, small kernel, small particle. See Corn, and cf. Garner, n., Garnet, Gram the chick-pea, Granule, Kernel.]

senses.d: To paint in imitation of the grain of wood, marble, etc.
To form (powder, sugar, etc.) into grains.
To take the hair off (skins); to soften and raise the grain of (leather, etc.).
To yield fruit.
To form grains, or to assume a granular form, as the result of crystallization; to granulate.
A branch of a tree; a stalk or stem of a plant.
A tine, prong, or fork.
A blade of a sword, knife, etc.
A thin piece of metal, used in a mold to steady a core.

Grain.etym: [See Groin a part of the body.]

senses.d: The mother of one's father or mother.
To give over; to make conveyance of; to give the possession or title of; to convey; — usually in answer to petition.
q: Grant me the place of this threshing floor.

senses.d: To bestow or confer, with or without compensation, particularly in answer to prayer or request; to give.
q: Wherefore did God grant me my request.

senses.d: To admit as true what is not yet satisfactorily proved; to yield belief to; to allow; to yield; to concede.
q: Grant that the Fates have firmed by their decree.

Grant.syn: To give; confer; bestow; convey; transfer; admit; allow; concede. See Give.
Grant.etym: [OE. graunten, granten, OF. graanter, craanter, creanter, to promise, yield, LL. creantare to promise, assure, for (assumed LL.) credentare to make believe, fr. L. credens, p. pr. of credere to believe. See Creed, Credit.]

senses.d: To assent; to consent.
The act of granting; a bestowing or conferring; concession; allowance; permission.
The yielding or admission of something in dispute.
The thing or property granted; a gift; a boon.
A transfer of property by deed or writing; especially, an appropriation or conveyance made by the government; as, a grant of land or of money; also, the deed or writing by which the transfer is made.

Grant.etym: [OE. grant, graunt, OF. graant, creant, promise, assurance. See Grant, v. t.]
