senses.d: A well-known edible berry growing in pendent clusters or bunches on the grapevine. The berries are smooth-skinned, have a juicy pulp, and are cultivated in great quantities for table use and for making wine and raisins.
The plant which bears this fruit; the grapevine.
A mangy tumor on the leg of a horse.
Grapeshot.

Grape.etym: [OF. grape, crape, bunch or cluster of grapes, F. grappe, akin to F. grappin grapnel, hook; fr. OHG. chrapfo hook, G. krapfen, akin to E. cramp. The sense seems to have come from the idea of clutching. Cf. Agraffe, Cramp, Grapnel, Grapple.]

senses.d: Popularly: Herbage; the plants which constitute the food of cattle and other beasts; pasture.
An endogenous plant having simple leaves, a stem generally jointed and tubular, the husks or glumes in pairs, and the seed single.
The season of fresh grass; spring.
q: Two years old next grass.

senses.d: Metaphorically used for what is transitory.
q: Surely the people is grass.

senses.d: for hay. South. Panicum Grus-galli.
pasture and hay. Agrostis, several species.
pasture. South. Cynodon Dactylon.
Same as Switch grass (below).
hay. North and West. Andropogon provincialis.
pasture. Poa compressa.
hay. Northwest. Aqropyrum glaucum.
Buchloë dectyloides

Grass.etym: [OE. gras, gres, gers, AS, græs, gærs; akin to OFries. gres, gers, OS., D., G., Icel., & Goth. gras, Dan. græs, Sw. gräs, and prob. to E. green, grow. Cf. Graze.]

senses.d: To cover with grass or with turf.
To expose, as flax, on the grass for bleaching, etc.
To bring to the grass or ground; to land; as, to grass a fish.
To produce grass.

Any jumping, orthopterous insect, of the families Acrididæ and Locustidæ. The species and genera are very numerous. The former family includes the Western grasshopper or locust (Caloptenus spretus), noted for the great extent of its ravages in the region beyond the Mississippi. In the Eastern United States the red-legged (Caloptenus femurrubrum and C. atlanis) are closely related species, but their ravages are less important. They are closely related to the migratory locusts of the Old World. See Locust.
In ordinary square or upright pianos of London make, the escapement lever or jack, so made that it can be taken out and replaced with the key; — called also the hopper.
Serving to gratify; agreeable.
A structure or frame containing parallel or crosed bars, with interstices; a kind of latticework, such as is used ia the windows of prisons and cloisters.
A frame or bed, or kind of basket, of iron bars, for holding fuel while burning.
To furnish with grates; to protect with a grating or crossbars; as, to grate a window.
To rub roughly or harshly, as one body against another, causing a harsh sound; as, to grate the teeth; to produce (a harsh sound) by rubbing.
q: On their hinges grate Harsh thunder.

senses.d: To reduce to small particles by rubbing with anything rough or indented; as, to grate a nutmeg.
To fret; to irritate; to offend.
q: News, my good lord Rome . . . grates me.

Grate.etym: [OF grater to scrape, scratch, F. gratter, LL. gratare, cratare; of German origin; cf. OHG. chrazzōn G. kratzen, D. krassen, Sw. Kratta, and perh. E. scratch.]

senses.d: To make a harsh sound by friction.
q: I had rather hear a brazen canstick turned, Or a dry wheel grate on the exletree.

senses.d: To produce the effect of rubbing with a hard rough material; to cause wearing, tearing, or bruising. Hence; To produce exasperation, soreness, or grief; to offend by oppression or importunity.
q: This grated harder upon the hearts of men.

senses.d: To clean, as a vessel's bottom, of barnacles, grass, etc., and pay it over with pitch; — so called because graves or greaves was formerly used for this purpose.
Of great weight; heavy; ponderous.
q: His shield grave and great.

senses.d: Of importance; momentous; weighty; influential; sedate; serious; — said of character, relations, etc.; as, grave deportment, character, influence, etc.
q: Most potent, grave, and reverend seigniors.
A grave and prudent law, full of moral equity.

senses.d: Not light or gay; solemn; sober; plain; as, a grave color; a grave face.
Not acute or sharp; low; deep; — said of sound; as, a grave note or key.
q: The thicker the cord or string, the more grave is the note or tone.

senses.d: Slow and solemn in movement.

Grave.syn: Solemn; sober; serious; sage; staid; demure; thoughtful; sedate; weighty; momentous; important.
Grave.etym: [F., fr. L. gravis heavy; cf. It. & Sp. grave heavy, grave. See Grief.]

senses.d: To dig. Chaucer.
q: He hath graven and digged up a pit.

senses.d: To carve or cut, as letters or figures, on some hard substance; to engrave.
q: Thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel.

senses.d: To carve out or give shape to, by cutting with a chisel; to sculpture; as, to grave an image.
q: With gold men may the hearte grave.

senses.d: To impress deeply (on the mind); to fix indelibly.
q: O! may they graven in thy heart remain.

senses.d: To entomb; to bury.
q: Lie full low, graved in the hollow ground.

Grave.etym: [AS. grafan to dig, grave, engrave; akin to OFries. greva, D. graven, G. graben, OHG. & Goth. graban, Dan. grabe, Sw. gräfva, Icel. grafa, but prob. not to Gr. γράφειν to write, E. graphic. Cf. Grave, n., Grove, n.]

senses.d: To write or delineate on hard substances, by means of incised lines; to practice engraving.
An excavation in the earth as a place of burial; also, any place of interment; a tomb; a sepulcher. Hence: Death; destruction.
q: He bad lain in the grave four days.

Grave.etym: [AS. gr?f, fr. grafan to dig; akin to D. & OS. graf, G. grab, Icel. gröf, Russ. grob' grave, coffin. See Grave to carve.]

senses.d: The clothes or dress in which the dead are interred.
Small stones, or fragments of stone; very small pebbles, often intermixed with particles of sand.
A deposit of small calculous concretions in the kidneys and the urinary or gall bladder; also, the disease of which they are a symptom.

Gravel.etym: [OF. gravele, akin to F. gr?ve a sandy shore, strand; of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. grouan gravel, W. gro coarse gravel, pebbles, and Skr. grāvan stone.]

senses.d: To cover with gravel; as, to gravel a walk.
To run (as a ship) upon the gravel or beach; to run aground; to cause to stick fast in gravel or sand.
q: When we were fallen into a place between two seas, they graveled the ship.
Willam the Conqueror . . . chanced as his arrival to be graveled; and one of his feet stuck so fast in the sand that he fell to the ground.

senses.d: To check or stop; to embarrass; to perplex.
q: When you were graveled for lack of matter.
The physician was so graveled and amazed withal, that he had not a word more to say.

senses.d: To hurt or lame (a horse) by gravel lodged between the shoe and foot.
Carved.
The sediment of melted tallow. Same as Greaves.
The act of cleaning a ship's bottom.
The act or art of carving figures in hard substances, esp. by incision or in intaglio.
That which is graved or carved.
q: Skillful to . . . grave any manner of graving.

senses.d: Impression, as upon the mind or heart.
q: New gravings upon their souls.

senses.d: The state of having weight; beaviness; as, the gravity of lead.
Sobriety of character or demeanor.
Importance, significance, dignity, etc; hence, seriousness; enormity; as, the gravity of an offense.
q: They derive an importance from . . . the gravity of the place where they were uttered.

senses.d: The tendency of a mass of matter toward a center of attraction; esp., the tendency of a body toward the center of the earth; terrestrial gravitation.
Lowness of tone; — opposed to acuteness.

Gravity.etym: [L. gravitas, fr. gravis heavy; cf. F. gravité. See Grave, a., Grief.]

senses.d: White mixed with black, as the color of pepper and salt, or of ashes, or of hair whitened by age; sometimes, a dark mixed color; as, the soft gray eye of a dove.
q: These gray and dun colors may be also produced by mixing whites and blacks.

senses.d: Gray-haired; gray-headed; of a gray color; hoary.
Old; mature; as, gray experience. Ames.

Gray.etym: [OE. gray, grey, AS. grǣg, grēg; akin to D. graauw, OHG. grāo, G. grau, Dan. graa, Sw. grå, Icel. grār.]

senses.d: A gray color; any mixture of white and black; also, a neutral or whitish tint.
An animal or thing of gray color, as a horse, a badger, or a kind of salmon.
q: Woe worth the chase, woe worth the day. That coats thy life, my gallant gray.

senses.d: Animal fat, as tallow or lard, especially when in a soft state; oily or unctuous matter of any kind.
An inflammation of a horse's heels, suspending the ordinary greasy secretion of the part, and producing dryness and scurfiness, followed by cracks, ulceration, and fungous excrescences.

Grease.etym: [OE. grese, grece, F. graisse; akin to gras fat, greasy, fr. LL. grassus thick, fat, gross, L. crassus. Cf. Crass.]

senses.d: To smear, anoint, or daub, with grease or fat; to lubricate; as, to grease the wheels of a wagon.
To bribe; to corrupt with presents.
q: The greased advocate that grinds the poor.

senses.d: To cheat or cozen; to overreach.
To affect (a horse) with grease, the disease.
Large in space; of much size; big; immense; enormous; expanded; — opposed to small and little; as, a great house, ship, farm, plain, distance, length.
Large in number; numerous; as, a great company, multitude, series, etc.
Long continued; lengthened in duration; prolonged in time; as, a great while; a great interval.
Superior; admirable; commanding; — applied to thoughts, actions, and feelings.
Endowed with extraordinary powers; uncommonly gifted; able to accomplish vast results; strong; powerful; mighty; noble; as, a great hero, scholar, genius, philosopher, etc.
Holding a chief position; elevated: lofty: eminent; distinguished; foremost; principal; as, great men; the great seal; the great marshal, etc.
q: He doth object I am too great of birth.

senses.d: Entitled to earnest consideration; weighty; important; as, a great argument, truth, or principle.
Pregnant; big (with young).
q: The ewes great with young.

senses.d: More than ordinary in degree; very considerable in degree; as, to use great caution; to be in great pain.
q: We have all Great cause to give great thanks.

senses.d: Older, younger, or more remote, by single generation; — often used before grand to indicate one degree more remote in the direct line of descent; as, great-grandfather (a grandfather's or a grandmother's father), great-grandson, etc.

Great.etym: [OE. gret, great, AS. greát; akin to OS. & LG. grōt, D. groot, OHG. grōz, G. gross. Cf. Groat the coin.]

senses.d: The whole; the gross; as, a contract to build a ship by the great.
In a great degree; much.
q: I will greatly multiply thy sorrow.

senses.d: Nobly; illustriously; magnanimously.
q: By a high fate thou greatly didst expire.

senses.d: The state, condition, or quality of being great; as, greatness of size, greatness of mind, power, etc.
Pride; haughtiness.
q: It is not of pride or greatness that he cometh not aboard your ships.

senses.d: A grove.
Armor for the leg below the knee; — usually in the plural.
To clean (a ship's bottom); to grave.
The sediment of melted tallow. It is made into cakes for dogs' food. In Scotland it is called cracklings.

Greaves.etym: [Cf. dial. Sw. grevar greaves, LG. greven, G. griebe, also AS. greofa pot. Cf. Gravy.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Greece; Greek.
A native or naturalized inhabitant of Greece; a Greek.
A jew who spoke Greek; a Hellenist.
One well versed in the Greek language, literature, or history.
In a greedy manner.
The quality of being greedy; vehement and selfish desire.
q: Fox in stealth, wolf in greediness.

senses.d: Having a keen appetite for food or drink; ravenous; voracious; very hungry; — followed by of; as, a lion that is greedy of his prey.
Having a keen desire for anything; vehemently desirous; eager to obtain; avaricious; as, greedy of gain.

Greedy.etym: [OE. gredi, AS. grǣdig, grēdig; akin to D. gretig, OS. grādag, OHG. grātag, Dan. graadig, OSw. gradig, grådig, Icel. grāðugr, Goth. grēdags greedy, grēdēn to be hungry; cf. Skr. gṛdh to be greedy. Cf. Greed.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to Greece or the Greeks; Grecian.

Greek.etym: [AS. grec, L. Graecus, Gr. ?: cf. F. grec. Cf. Grecian.]

senses.d: A native, or one of the people, of Greece; a Grecian; also, the language of Greece.
A swindler; a knave; a cheat.
q: Without a confederate the . . . game of baccarat does not . . . offer many chances for the Greek.

senses.d: Something unintelligible; as, it was all Greek to me.
Having the color of grass when fresh and growing; resembling that color of the solar spectrum which is between the yellow and the blue; verdant; emerald.
Having a sickly color; wan.
q: To look so green and pale.

senses.d: Full of life and vigor; fresh and vigorous; new; recent; as, a green manhood; a green wound.
q: As valid against such an old and beneficent government as against . . . the greenest usurpation.

senses.d: Not ripe; immature; not fully grown or ripened; as, green fruit, corn, vegetables, etc.
Not roasted; half raw.
q: We say the meat is green when half roasted.

senses.d: Immature in age or experience; young; raw; not trained; awkward; as, green in years or judgment.
q: I might be angry with the officious zeal which supposes that its green conceptions can instruct my gray hairs.

senses.d: Not seasoned; not dry; containing its natural juices; as, green wood, timber, etc.

Green.etym: [OE. grene, AS. gr?ne; akin to D. groen, OS. gr?ni, OHG. gruoni, G. gr?n, Dan. & Sw. gr?n, Icel. gr?nn; fr. the root of E. grow. See Grow.]

senses.d: The color of growing plants; the color of the solar spectrum intermediate between the yellow and the blue.
A grassy plain or plat; a piece of ground covered with verdant herbage; as, the village green.
q: O'er the smooth enameled green.

senses.d: Fresh leaves or branches of trees or other plants; wreaths; — usually in the plural.
q: In that soft season when descending showers Call forth the greens, and wake the rising flowers.

senses.d: pl. Leaves and stems of young plants, as spinach, beets, etc., which in their green state are boiled for food.
Any substance or pigment of a green color.
To make green.
q: Great spring before Greened all the year.

senses.d: To become or grow green.
q: By greening slope and singing flood.

senses.d: Somewhat green; having a tinge of green; as, a greenish yellow.
The quality of being green; viridity; verdancy; as, the greenness of grass, or of a meadow.
Freshness; vigor; newness.
Immaturity; unripeness; as, the greenness of fruit; inexperience; as, the greenness of youth.
Great.
To weep; to cry; to lament.

Greet.etym: [OE. greten, AS. grǣtan, grētan; akin to Icel. grāta, Sw. gråta, Dan. græde, Goth. grēctan; cf. Skr. hrād to sound, roar. √50.]

senses.d: Mourning.

To address with salutations or expressions of kind wishes; to salute; to hail; to welcome; to accost with friendship; to pay respects or compliments to, either personally or through the intervention of another, or by writing or token.
q: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.

senses.d: To come upon, or meet, as with something that makes the heart glad.
q: In vain the spring my senses greets.

senses.d: To accost; to address.

Greet.etym: [OE. greten, AS. grētan to address, approach; akin to OS. grōtian, LG. gröten, D. groeten, OHG. gruozzen, G. grüssen. √50.]

senses.d: To meet and give salutations.
q: There greet in silence, as the dead are wont, And sleep in peace.

senses.d: Greeting.
Expression of kindness or joy; salutation at meeting; a compliment from one absent.
q: Write to him . . . gentle adieus and greetings.

senses.d: A slender, graceful breed of dogs, remarkable for keen sight and swiftness. It is one of the oldest varieties known, and is figured on the Egyptian monuments.

Greyhound.etym: [OE. graihund, greihound, greahund, grihond, Icel. greyhundr; grey greyhound + hundr dog; cf. AS. grīghund. The origin of the first syllable is unknown.]

senses.d: A swift steamer, esp. an ocean steamer.
Pain of mind on account of something in the past; mental suffering arising from any cause, as misfortune, loss of friends, misconduct of one's self or others, etc.; sorrow; sadness.
q: The mother was so afflicted at the loss of a fine boy, . . . that she died for grief of it.

senses.d: Cause of sorrow or pain; that which afficts or distresses; trial; grievance.
q: Be factious for redress of all these griefs.

senses.d: Physical pain, or a cause of it; malady.
q: This grief (cancerous ulcers) hastened the end of that famous mathematician, Mr. Harriot.

Grief.syn: Affiction; sorrow; distress; sadness; trial; grievance.
Grief.etym: [OE. grief, gref, OF. grief, gref, F. grief, L. gravis heavy; akin to Gr. βαρύσ, Skr. guru, Goth. kaúrus. Cf. Barometer, Grave, a., Grieve, Gooroo.]

senses.d: A cause of uneasiness and complaint; a wrong done and suffered; that which gives ground for remonstrance or resistance, as arising from injustice, tyranny, etc.; injury.
Grieving; grief; affliction.
q: The . . . grievance of a mind unreasonably yoked.

senses.d: A manager of a farm, or overseer of any work; a reeve; a manorial bailiff.
q: Their children were horsewhipped by the grieve.

senses.d: To occasion grief to; to wound the sensibilities of; to make sorrowful; to cause to suffer; to afflict; to hurt; to try.
q: Grieve not the Holy Spirit of God.
The maidens grieved themselves at my concern.

senses.d: To sorrow over; as, to grieve one's fate.

Grieve.etym: [OE. greven, OF. grever, fr. L. gravare to burden, oppress, fr. gravis heavy. See Grief.]

senses.d: To feel grief; to be in pain of mind on account of an evil; to sorrow; to mourn; — often followed by at, for, or over.
q: Do not you grieve at this.

senses.d: Sad; sorrowful; causing grief.
The act of causing grief; the state of being grieved.
Causing grief or sorrow; painful; afflictive; hard to bear; offensive; harmful.
q: The famine was grievous in the land.
The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight.

senses.d: Characterized by great atrocity; heinous; aggravated; flagitious; as, a grievous sin.
Full of, or expressing, grief; showing great sorrow or affliction; as, a grievous cry.

Grievous.etym: [OF. grevous, grevos, LL. gravosus. See Grief.]

senses.d: To reduce to powder by friction, as in a mill, or with the teeth; to crush into small fragments; to produce as by the action of millstones.
q: Take the millstones, and grind meal.

senses.d: To wear down, polish, or sharpen, by friction; to make smooth, sharp, or pointed; to whet, as a knife or drill; to rub against one another, as teeth, etc.
To oppress by severe exactions; to harass.
q: To grind the subject or defraud the prince.

senses.d: To study hard for examination.

Grind.etym: [AS. grindan; perh. akin to L. frendere to gnash, grind. Cf. Grist.]

senses.d: To perform the operation of grinding something; to turn the millstones.
q: Send thee Into the common prison, there to grind.

senses.d: To become ground or pulverized by friction; as, this corn grinds well.
To become polished or sharpened by friction; as, glass grinds smooth; steel grinds to a sharp edge.
To move with much difficulty or friction; to grate.
To perform hard and distasteful service; to drudge; to study hard, as for an examination.
The act of reducing to powder, or of sharpening, by friction.
Any severe continuous work or occupation; esp., hard and uninteresting study.
A hard student; a dig.
One who, or that which, grinds.
One of the double teeth, used to grind or masticate the food; a molar.
The restless flycatcher (Seisura inquieta) of Australia; — called also restless thrush and volatile thrush. It makes a noise like a scissors grinder, to which the name alludes.
from Grind.
To give forth a low, moaning sound in breathing; to utter a groan, as in pain, in sorrow, or in derision; to moan.
q: For we . . . do groan, being burdened.
He heard the groaning of the oak.

senses.d: To strive after earnestly, as with groans.
q: Nothing but holy, pure, and clear, Or that which groaneth to be so.

Groan.etym: [OE. gronen, granen, granien, AS. gr�nian, fr. the root of grennian to grin. √35. See 2d Grin, and cf. Grunt.]

senses.d: To affect by groans.
A low, moaning sound; usually, a deep, mournful sound uttered in pain or great distress; sometimes, an expression of strong disapprobation; as, the remark was received with groans.
q: Such groans of roaring wind and rain.
The wretched animal heaved forth such groans.

senses.d: To feel with or use the hands; to handle.

To search or attempt to find something in the dark, or, as a blind person, by feeling; to move about hesitatingly, as in darkness or obscurity; to feel one's way, as with the hands, when one can not see.
q: We grope for the wall like the blind.
To grope a little longer among the miseries and sensualities ot a worldly life.

Grope.etym: [OE. gropen, gropien, grapien, AS. grāpian to touch, grope, fr. grīpan to gripe. See Gripe.]

senses.d: To search out by feeling in the dark; as, we groped our way at midnight.
To examine; to test; to sound.
q: Felix gropeth him, thinking to have a bribe.

senses.d: A heavy silk with a dull finish; as, gros de Naples; gros de Tours.
Great; large; bulky; fat; of huge size; excessively large.
q: A gross body of horse under the Duke.

senses.d: Coarse; rough; not fine or delicate.
Not easily aroused or excited; not sensitive in perception or feeling; dull; witless.
q: Tell her of things that no gross ear can hear.

senses.d: Expressing, or originating in, animal or sensual appetites; hence, coarse, vulgar, low, obscene, or impure.
q: The terms which are delicate in one age become gross in the next.

senses.d: Thick; dense; not attenuated; as, a gross medium.
Great; palpable; serious; vagrant; shameful; as, a gross mistake; gross injustice; gross negligence.
Whole; entire; total; without deduction; as, the gross sum, or gross amount, the gross weight; — opposed to net.

Gross.etym: [F. gros, L. grossus, perh. fr. L. crassus thick, dense, fat, E. crass, cf. Skr. grathita tied together, wound up, hardened. Cf. Engross, Grocer, Grogram.]

senses.d: The main body; the chief part, bulk, or mass.
q: For the gross of the people, they are considered as a mere herd of cattle.

senses.d: The number of twelve dozen; twelve times twelve; as, a gross of bottles; ten gross of pens.

Gross.etym: [F. gros (in sense 1), grosse (in sense 2). See Gross, a.]

senses.d: The surface of the earth; the outer crust of the globe, or some indefinite portion of it.
q: There was not a man to till the ground.
The fire ran along upon the ground.

senses.d: A floor or pavement supposed to rest upon the earth.

Any definite portion of the earth's surface; region; territory; country. Hence: A territory appropriated to, or resorted to, for a particular purpose; the field or place of action; as, a hunting or fishing ground; a play ground.
q: From . . . old Euphrates, to the brook that parts Egypt from Syrian ground.

senses.d: Land; estate; possession; field; esp. (pl.), the gardens, lawns, fields, etc., belonging to a homestead; as, the grounds of the estate are well kept.
q: Thy next design is on thy neighbor's grounds.

senses.d: The basis on which anything rests; foundation. Hence: The foundation of knowledge, belief, or conviction; a premise, reason, or datum; ultimate or first principle; cause of existence or occurrence; originating force or agency; as, the ground of my hope.

That surface upon which the figures of a composition are set, and which relieves them by its plainness, being either of one tint or of tints but slightly contrasted with one another; as, crimson Bowers on a white ground.
A gummy composition spread over the surface of a metal to be etched, to prevent the acid from eating except where an opening is made by the needle.
One of the pieces of wood, flush with the plastering, to which moldings, etc., are attached; — usually in the plural.
A composition in which the bass, consisting of a few bars of independent notes, is continually repeated to a varying melody.
q: On that ground I'll build a holy descant.

senses.d: A conducting connection with the earth, whereby the earth is made part of an electrical circuit.
Sediment at the bottom of liquors or liquids; dregs; lees; feces; as, coffee grounds.
The pit of a theater.

Ground.etym: [OE. ground, grund, AS. grund; akin to D. grond, OS., G., Sw., & Dan. grund, Icel. grunnr bottom, Goth. grundus (in composition); perh. orig. meaning, dust, gravel, and if so perh. akin to E. grind.]

senses.d: To lay, set, or run, on the ground.
To found; to fix or set, as on a foundation, reason, or principle; to furnish a ground for; to fix firmly.
q: Being rooted and grounded in love.
So far from warranting any inference to the existence of a God, would, on the contrary, ground even an argument to his negation.

senses.d: To instruct in elements or first principles.
To connect with the ground so as to make the earth a part of an electrical circuit.
To cover with a ground, as a copper plate for etching (see Ground, n., 5); or as paper or other materials with a uniform tint as a preparation for ornament.
To run aground; to strike the bottom and remain fixed; as, the ship grounded on the bar.
A smaller group of trees than a forest, and without underwood, planted, or growing naturally as if arranged by art; a wood of small extent.

Grove.etym: [AS. graf, fr. grafan to dig. The original sense seems to have been a lane cut through trees. See Grave, v., and cf. Groove.]

senses.d: To increase in size by a natural and organic process; to increase in bulk by the gradual assimilation of new matter into the living organism; — said of animals and vegetables and their organs.
To increase in any way; to become larger and stronger; to be augmented; to advance; to extend; to wax; to accrue.
q: Winter began to grow fast on.
Even just the sum that I do owe to you Is growing to me by Antipholus.

senses.d: To spring up and come to maturity in a natural way; to be produced by vegetation; to thrive; to flourish; as, rice grows in warm countries.
q: Where law faileth, error groweth.

senses.d: To pass from one state to another; to result as an effect from a cause; to become; as, to grow pale.
q: For his mind Had grown Suspicion's sanctuary.

senses.d: To become attached or fixed; to adhere.
q: Our knees shall kneel till to the ground they grow.

Grow.syn: To become; increase; enlarge; augment; improve; expand; extend.
Grow.etym: [AS. grōwan; akin to D. groeijen, Icel. grōa, Dan. groe, Sw. gro. Cf. Green, Grass.]

senses.d: To cause to grow; to cultivate; to produce; as, to grow a crop; to grow wheat, hops, or tobacco.

Grow.syn: To raise; to cultivate. See Raise, v. t., 3.

senses.d: The process of growing; the gradual increase of an animal or a vegetable body; the development from a seed, germ, or root, to full size or maturity; increase in size, number, frequency, strength, etc.; augmentation; advancement; production; prevalence or influence; as, the growth of trade; the growth of power; the growth of intemperance. Idle weeds are fast in growth.
That which has grown or is growing; anything produced; product; consequence; effect; result.
q: Nature multiplies her fertile growth.

senses.d: To look upon with desire to possess or to appropriate; to envy (one) the possession of; to begrudge; to covet; to give with reluctance; to desire to get back again; — followed by the direct object only, or by both the direct and indirect objects.
q: Tis not in thee To grudge my pleasures, to cut off my train.
I have often heard the Presbyterians say, they did not grudge us our employments.
They have grudged us contribution.

senses.d: To hold or harbor with malicious disposition or purpose; to cherish enviously.
q: Perish they That grudge one thought against your majesty !

Grudge.etym: [OE. grutchen, gruchen, grochen, to murmur, grumble, OF. grochier, grouchier, grocier, groucier; cf. Icel. krytja to murmur, krutr a murmur, or E. grunt.]

senses.d: To be covetous or envious; to show discontent; to murmur; to complain; to repine; to be unwilling or reluctant.
q: Grudge not one against another.
He eats his meat without grudging.

senses.d: To feel compunction or grief.
Sullen malice or malevolence; cherished malice, enmity, or dislike; ill will; an old cause of hatred or quarrel.
q: Esau had conceived a mortal grudge and enmity against his brother Jacob.
The feeling may not be envy; it may not be imbittered by a grudge.

senses.d: Slight symptom of disease.
q: Our shaken monarchy, that now lies . . . struggling against the grudges of more dreaded calamities.

Grudge.syn: Pique; aversion; dislike; ill will; hatred; spite. See Pique.

senses.d: In a grudging manner.

To protect from danger; to secure against surprise, attack, or injury; to keep in safety; to defend; to shelter; to shield from surprise or attack; to protect by attendance; to accompany for protection; to care for.
q: For Heaven still guards the right.

senses.d: To keep watch over, in order to prevent escape or restrain from acts of violence, or the like.
To protect the edge of, esp. with an ornamental border; hence, to face or ornament with lists, laces, etc.
q: The body of your discourse is sometime guarded with fragments, and the guards are but slightly basted on neither.

senses.d: To fasten by binding; to gird.

Guard.syn: To defend; protect; shield; keep; watch.
Guard.etym: [OF. guarder, garder, warder, F. garder, fr. OHG. wart�n to be on the watch, await, G. marten. See Ward, v. & n., and cf. Guard, n.]

senses.d: To watch by way of caution or defense; to be cautious; to be in a state or position of defense or safety; as, careful persons guard against mistakes.
One who, or that which, guards from injury, danger, exposure, or attack; defense; protection.
q: His greatness was no guard to bar heaven's shaft.

senses.d: A man, or body of men, stationed to protect or control a person or position; a watch; a sentinel.
q: The guard which kept the door of the king's house.

senses.d: One who has charge of a mail coach or a railway train; a conductor.
Any fixture or attachment designed to protect or secure against injury, soiling, or defacement, theft or loss
A posture of defense in fencing, and in bayonet and saber exercise.
An expression or admission intended to secure against objections or censure.
q: They have expressed themselves with as few guards and restrictions as I.

senses.d: Watch; heed; care; attention; as, to keep guard.
The fibrous sheath which covers the phragmacone of the Belemnites.

Guard.syn: Defense; shield; protection; safeguard; convoy; escort; care; attention; watch; heed.
Guard.etym: [OF. guarde, F. garde; of German origin; cf. OHG. wart, warto, one who watches, warta a watching, Goth. wardja watchman. See Guard, v. t.]

senses.d: A sharper; a rogue.
A visitor; a person received and entertained in one's house or at one's table; a visitor entertained without pay.
q: To cheer his guests, whom he had stayed that night.
True friendship's laws are by this rule exprest. Welcome the coming, speed the parting guest.

Guest.etym: [OE. gest, AS. gæst, gest; akin to OS., D., & G. gast, Icel. gestr, Sw. gäst, Dan. Gjäst, Goth. gasts, Russ. goste, and to L. hostis enemy, stranger; the meaning stranger is the older one, but the root is unknown. Cf. Host an army, Hostile.]

senses.d: To receive or entertain hospitably.
To be, or act the part of, a guest.
q: And tell me, best of princes, who he was That guested here so late.

senses.d: Any insect that lives in the nest of another without compulsion and usually not as a parasite.
An inquiline.
To lead or direct in a way; to conduct in a course or path; to pilot; as, to guide a traveler.
q: I wish . . . you 'ld guide me to your sovereign's court.

senses.d: To regulate and manage; to direct; to order; to superintend the training or education of; to instruct and influence intellectually or morally; to train.
q: He will guide his affairs with discretion.
The meek will he guide in judgment.

Guide.etym: [OE. guiden, gyden, F. guiaer, It. guidare; prob. of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. ritan to watch over, give heed to, Icel. viti signal, AS. witan to know. The word prob. meant, to indicate, point to, and hence, to show the way. Cf. Wit, Guy a rope, Gye.]

senses.d: A person who leads or directs another in his way or course, as in a strange land; one who exhibits points of interest to strangers; a conductor; also, that which guides; a guidebook.
One who, or that which, directs another in his conduct or course of life; a director; a regulator.
q: He will be our guide, even unto death.

senses.d: Any contrivance, especially one having a directing edge, surface, or channel, for giving direction to the motion of anything, as water, an instrument, or part of a machine, or for directing the hand or eye, as of an operator

A noncommissioned officer or soldier placed on the directing flank of each subdivision of a column of troops, or at the end of a line, to mark the pivots, formations, marches, and alignments in tactics.

Guide.etym: [OE. giae, F. guide, It. guida. See Guide, v. t.]

senses.d: Craft; deceitful cunning; artifice; duplicity; wile; deceit; treachery.
q: Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile.
To wage by force or guile eternal war.

Guile.etym: [OE. guile, gile, OF. guile; of German origin, and the same word as E. wile. See Wile.]

senses.d: To disguise or conceal; to deceive or delude.

The criminality and consequent exposure to punishment resulting from willful disobedience of law, or from morally wrong action; the state of one who has broken a moral or political law; crime; criminality; offense against right.
q: Satan had not answer, but stood struck With guilt of his own sin.

senses.d: Exposure to any legal penalty or forfeiture.
q: A ship incurs guilt by the violation of a blockade.

Guilt.etym: [OE. gilt, gult, AS. gylt, crime; probably originally signifying, the fine or mulct paid for an offence, and afterward the offense itself, and akin to AS. gieldan to pay, E. yield. See Yield, v. t.]

senses.d: The quality or state of being guilty.
Free from guilt; innocent.
q: The Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

senses.d: Without experience or trial; unacquainted (with).
q: Such gardening tools, as art, yet rude, Guiltless of fire, had formed.

senses.d: Having incurred guilt; criminal; morally delinquent; wicked; chargeable with, or responsible for, something censurable; justly exposed to penalty; — used with of, and usually followed by the crime, sometimes by the punishment.
q: They answered and said, He is guilty of death.
Nor he, nor you, were guilty of the strife.

senses.d: Evincing or indicating guilt; involving guilt; as, a guilty look; a guilty act; a guilty feeling.
Conscious; cognizant.
Condemned to payment.
A hollow place in the earth; an abyss; a deep chasm or basin,
q: He then surveyed Hell and the gulf between.
Between us and you there is a great gulf fixed.

senses.d: That which swallows; the gullet.
That which swallows irretrievably; a whirlpool; a sucking eddy.
q: A gulf of ruin, swallowing gold.

senses.d: A portion of an ocean or sea extending into the land; a partially land-locked sea; as, the Gulf of Mexico.
A large deposit of ore in a lode.

Gulf.etym: [F. golfe, It. golfo, fr. Gr. � bosom, bay, gulf, LGr. �.]

senses.d: To issue with violence and rapidity, as a fluid; to rush forth as a fluid from confinement; to flow copiously.
q: He smote the rock that the waters gushed out.
A sea of blood gushed from the gaping wound.

senses.d: To make a sentimental or untimely exhibition of affection; to display enthusiasm in a silly, demonstrative manner.

Gush.etym: [OE. guschen, cf. Icel. gusa and gjsa, also D. gucsen; perh. akin to AS. geótan to pour, G. giessen, Goth. giutan, E. gut. Cf. Found to cast.]

senses.d: A sudden and violent issue of a fluid from an inclosed plase; an emission of a liquid in a large quantity, and with force; the fluid thus emitted; a rapid outpouring of anything; as, a gush of song from a bird.
q: The gush of springs, An fall of lofty foundains.

senses.d: A sentimental exhibition of affection or enthusiasm, etc.; effusive display of sentiment.
A narrow passage of water; as, the Gut of Canso.
An intenstine; a bowel; the whole alimentary canal; the enteron; (pl.) bowels; entrails.
One of the prepared entrails of an animal, esp. of a sheep, used for various purposes. See Catgut.
The sac of silk taken from a silkworm (when ready to spin its cocoon), for the purpose of drawing it out into a thread. This, when dry, is exceedingly strong, and is used as the snood of a fish line.

Gut.etym: [OE. gut, got, AS. gut, prob. orig., a channel, and akin to geótan to pour. See FOUND to cast.]

senses.d: To take out the bowels from; to eviscerate.
To plunder of contents; to destroy or remove the interior or contents of; as, a mob gutted the house.
q: Tom Brown, of facetious memory, having gutted a proper name of its vowels, used it as freely as he pleased.

senses.d: A channel at the eaves of a roof for conveying away the rain; an eaves channel; an eaves trough.
A small channel at the roadside or elsewhere, to lead off surface water.
q: Gutters running with ale.

senses.d: Any narrow channel or groove; as, a gutter formed by erosion in the vent of a gun from repeated firing.

Gutter.etym: [OE. gotere, OF. goutiere, F. gouttière, fr. OF. gote, goute, drop, F. goutte, fr. L. gutta.]

senses.d: To cut or form into small longitudinal hollows; to channel.
To supply with a gutter or gutters.
To become channeled, as a candle when the flame flares in the wind.
